title: Celebrity Has Become a Jobs Program
excerpt: Recently, an Instagram carousel by a long-lost acquaintance who was beach- and boat-hopping with a glittery squad of people I didn’t recognize crossed my feed
body: Recently, an Instagram carousel by a long-lost acquaintance who was beach- and boat-hopping with a glittery squad of people I didn’t recognize crossed my feed
I figured they were moneyed Millennials with regular jobs—until I discovered that several of them had followings in the high five figures, and one had more than 3 million
As it turns out, they were neither civilians nor stars

They were “Who”s: a category of low-tier celebrities, including influencers, reality stars, and podcasters—and commonly all three at once—whose names prompt you to ask: “Who?” The binary between “Who”s and “Them”s—the latter being A-listers your parents might recognize, such as Beyoncé and Tom Cruise—was invented by Bobby Finger and Lindsey Weber

Their podcast, Who? Weekly , bills itself as a show that covers “everything you need to know about celebrities you don’t.” After a decade on the beat, the pair have distilled their insights into a new book, I Want to Be Famous: When Everybody and Nobody Is a Celebrity , which offers a comprehensive theory of how the internet and social media transformed everyone into someone—and therefore, no one
That theory has surprising implications for the labor market at large

As social-media platforms have made it seem easy to monetize attention, professionals in industries where fame has not historically been a credential have come to face growing pressure to create and optimize their online brand

Personal branding, once almost exclusively the concern of genuine celebrities and more recently a job for social-media influencers, is now something a junior accounting executive is encouraged to think about

Sophie Bishop, a professor in media and communication at the University of Leeds, in England, calls this structural shift “influencer creep” —a phenomenon that has caused more swaths of the economy to function like the attention-hungry world that Who? Weekly dissects

No matter how staunchly we may wish to resist the fusion of work and life, we are what we do, and our job is to be a “Who.” Who? Weekly was launched in 2016 as a lighthearted but often trenchant analysis of fame at a time when social media was beginning to democratize the concept

Finger and Weber were both young entertainment journalists; as they write in I Want to Be Famous , they wanted a venue in which to grumble about celebrities turning away from traditional media and toward social platforms, where they could exercise more image control
Finger and Weber’s real innovation, however, was the system of Whos and Thems

Whos are thirsty for the attention that Thems already have and will shamelessly do or plug anything to get it. “By the end of the 2010s,” the authors write, “it seemed like every reality star, aspiring actor or musician, and TikTok influencer was supplementing their creative income with a post promoting a vibrator, supplement, gambling service, or alcoholic beverage.” [ Read more: The celebrity clock is getting rewired ] But as I Want to Be Famous reveals, social-media culture has changed so much that even Thems can no longer resist shilling for brands online

When Jennifer Aniston joined Instagram, in 2019, her first post was a selfie with her Friends co-stars. “It was a charming (if brief) glimpse into the personal life of one of our most private celebrities,” Finger and Weber write: “The purity of her feed was short-lived, however

Today, you can see ads for SkinnyPop popcorn among those intimate photos with friends because now everyone is free to sell stuff in this brave new world, without the fear of selling out.” Last month, another Them joined Instagram: the Oscar-winning actor Jennifer Lawrence, who in a video warned fans to be nice, or she’d quit
A couple of weeks later, Lawrence posted a carousel with grainy photos that were, in part, normal-person coded: There she was, eating a corn dog and riding the Tower of Terror
Except she was also at a Dior fashion show in Paris—right, she’s a movie star. “Thank you @dior and @jonathan.anderson for the most beautiful show ever,” she wrote in the caption
Maybe Lawrence joined the platform for the same reasons we all did: to make internet friends jealous with vacation pics
Or maybe her long-running role as a brand ambassador for Dior now requires her to broker attention online
We can’t know why anyone posts anything: for love or money, connection or commerce

But last week, Lawrence shared low-res, behind-the-scenes snapshots of her hairstyles in various movies, and updated her Instagram bio with a link to her new hair-care brand. [ Read more: The celebrity machine never dies ] Who? Weekly chronicles the rise of online attention and the decline of offline mystique
A 2024 post on the Harvard Business School blog offers an example

Branding yourself as a “financial analyst with high emotional intelligence who loves to ski,” the author argues, can help you find opportunities “that align with your authentic self.” The post also suggests that a job seeker might “promote your value” by using “a mix of paid, owned, and earned media.” What this means is that, to really get your mug in front of hiring managers and corporate recruiters, you should pay to amplify material that communicates your professional viability
Some Gen Z job seekers are using Instagram and TikTok to pitch themselves to potential employers
A 2025 survey found that 46 percent of Gen Z respondents had landed a job or an internship through TikTok
And LinkedIn, once a straitlaced professional networking site, now also functions something like Instagram for the corporate class
The idea is that becoming a platform personality through personal posts or videos will juice the algorithm and thus woo recruiters

The rise of the LinkedInfluencer is emblematic of the act of self-promotion becoming more front-facing: As Brooke Erin Duffy, a communication professor at Cornell University, asked in a June interview with The New York Times , “What does it mean for the rest of us who are living, working and spending our time in these sites where everything we see has this ethos of self promotion?” Companies including Starbucks and IBM have launched so-called employee-creator programs, initiatives that offers everyday workers rewards for serving as in-house posters. “We’re giving them a way to become influencers,” a July press release by Gap Inc. boasted about one such initiative
But the imperative to build followers stretches across corporate tiers

Jon Gray, the president and chief operating officer of Blackstone —one of the largest commercial landlords in the world—has gone viral on LinkedIn with relatably goofy videos of himself running; the platform’s editor in chief and vice president of content, Dan Roth, recently bragged that Gray has “become a creator.” How odd to feel sympathy for a billionaire: Somehow, he too is furiously—literally—running on the content hamster wheel. [ Read more: So a C-list celebrity is selling your house? ] Finger and Weber point out that, until recently, a professional working for a major corporation could count on a fairly linear career path

The same wasn’t true for someone like a reality star, who needed to rely on media access to sustain their fame and find new opportunities; they might start a lifestyle brand, for instance, in service of becoming what the authors call a “working Who.” Plenty of jobs don’t appear to be succumbing to this shift, at least not yet; your Instagram algorithm might surface the odd plumbing influencer, but your leaky faucet is unlikely to get fixed under the flattering glare of a ring light

Influencer culture has gone only so far in reshaping the labor market in its image, but as the corporate world adopts its practices, there is a growing incentive for you to become your own kind of “working Who”—and, in turn, to help reinforce the idea that people are products.

title: The Temporary Pleasure of Conversation
excerpt: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight
body: This is an edition of The Wonder Reader, a newsletter in which our editors recommend a set of stories to spark your curiosity and fill you with delight
Sign up here to get it every Saturday morning
Conversation, Charlie Tyson wrote in 2023, is by nature fleeting

He quotes Virginia Woolf: “It flies up the chimney,” she once said, “and is gone.” This perspective may be comforting for people who spend hours after a social interaction perseverating over that one joke that didn’t quite land
But Woolf’s remark doesn’t necessarily imply that conversation is meaningless

Understanding that conversations are temporary, that they fly up the chimney to make room for new ones, can help us talk to one another more honestly. “In the twists of talk, we open ourselves to others and allow our interior to be subtly reshaped,” Tyson wrote in his review of a book on the subject

The benefits of conversation are constantly threatened by modern life—by the pull of a phone notification during lunch with a friend, by the impulse to text instead of call, and perhaps most dramatically, by AI’s promise to obviate the human need for talking
Woolf’s description of language might make it seem replaceable, but this transient quality is precisely what makes talking an essential part of life
Language is something we are creating, demolishing, and creating again, every second of every day—a distinctly human act

title: AI Terrorism Is Just Terrorism
excerpt: The War on Terror coincided with the rise of the internet, when freshly concerning digital attacks became known as cyberterrorism
body: The War on Terror coincided with the rise of the internet, when freshly concerning digital attacks became known as cyberterrorism
Now a new threat has appeared: AI terrorism
Over the past few years, reports from governments , intergovernmental organizations , and think tanks have warned that AI is likely to fuel terrorist activity, demanding preparation and response

In 2021, the United Nations Office of Counter-Terrorism co-published a report on the “malicious use of artificial intelligence for terrorist purposes.” Cyberattacks such as malware and intrusion featured heavily, as did physical attacks via autonomous vehicles, facial-recognition spoofing, deepfakes, and—the coronavirus pandemic was still raging—engineered biological weapons

Earlier, in 2019 and 2020 , the Middlebury Institute of International Studies published two reports on the risks that language models, still mostly unheard-of at the time, would pose to propaganda and radicalization

And just this week, a group of Harvard Kennedy School researchers published a working paper that assumes that the “first major AI-enabled terrorism event” is a credible threat and speculates how it might come about

Cyberterrorism was already a confusing term, partly because hacking or disabling computer infrastructure might be carried out by state actors and without violence—properties that aren’t normally associated with terrorism
Among the reasons terrorism is bad, a very minor one is that the term has no fixed definition
In revolutionary France, it referred to violence exercised by the Jacobin state, in many cases by guillotine
By the late 19th century, it had shifted to the nonstate violence of anarchist would-be revolutionaries
Terrorism began to overlap with independence movements in the 20th century, drawing it closer to separatist conflict or guerrilla warfare
By the late 20th century, this ideological motivation for terrorism became mandatory
Terrorism amounted to violence designed to produce a psychological effect
The hijackings and hostage crises of the 1970s exemplify this revised purpose
So do domestic attacks, such as that of Timothy McVeigh, who bombed an Oklahoma City federal building in 1995

Today, a quarter century after the September 11 attacks, terrorism often carries a political judgment instead of describing an act or a type of actor: Nearly any adversary whatsoever might be called a “terrorist” now

Given the slippage of the term, AI is, in a way, terroristic by nature: It threatens to take your job, steal your money, ruin your children’s education, eradicate art and culture, take away your health care, colonize your town, destroy the climate, make electronics forever unaffordable

You have also been told that AI is inevitable—and that only immensely wealthy Silicon Valley companies, possibly run by sociopathic leaders, have the resources and talent to advance it (which they must do, even if it means the destruction of humankind)
But the older sense of terrorism still persists

The technology could also facilitate, in addition to the familiar chaos that AI threatens to unleash, terrorism in the sense of state- or nonstate-enacted violence or disruption, such as disabling your electric grid and unleashing a bioweapon at your workplace. [ Ian Bogost: The thrill of wanting AI to destroy the world ] The people who study AI terrorism raise different concerns than those raised by whistleblowers inside the AI industry—or AI leaders themselves
Superintelligent-AI-driven extinction events do not top the list of risks, nor do the rogue AI agents that might, in theory, become autonomous

Instead, researchers, intelligence officials, and scenario planners seem principally interested in the ways that AI might allow bad actors to carry out more sophisticated activities with reduced effort
The Las Vegas Cybertruck bomber, for example, asked ChatGPT for advice about how to detonate an explosion, a use that suggests terrorists might be stupid in addition to being enterprising
Today’s frontier AI models are powerful, cheap, and widely available
They can accomplish (or help accomplish, or appear to accomplish) many types of tasks without having been explicitly designed to do so
Criminals, terrorists, and even governments have tended to use existing communication, transportation, and industrial infrastructure to do bad things
This conclusion is both reasonable and a bit humdrum
Consequently, most of the reports on AI terrorism that I have read are conservative in their concerns
They stress that carrying out acts of violence or other physical attacks is difficult and that AI can’t magically solve those problems

They are, perhaps, responding to years of cyberterrorism-threat overstatement, the most famous example of which is the idea of an “electronic Pearl Harbor”—a devastating attack on digital infrastructure that incapacitates the nation

That metaphor, which has been in circulation since at least 1999 , was made more concrete in 2012, when then–Defense Secretary Leon Panetta warned Congress about a “cyber Pearl Harbor” that “could be as destructive as the terrorist attack on 9/11.” Many international-policy experts have argued that cyber Pearl Harbor amounts to a mixed metaphor
The attack on Pearl Harbor was an intricately planned act of state warfare, not a rogue operation
More likely, smaller cybersecurity incidents could cascade into bigger ones, or cause unpredictable secondary effects
Real, damaging cyberattacks on physical infrastructure have been possible for many years
AI’s role in cyberterrorism is likely to be the same as the internet’s: an amplified capacity to produce and disseminate propaganda, confusion, and political manipulation
Panetta justified the warning about a cyber Pearl Harbor on the grounds that the risk was possible even if it wasn’t plausible
A similar justification appears to motivate the Harvard Kennedy School researchers in their paper
The co-authors describe their methodology as a “pre-mortem,” which involves assuming that such an event has taken place and working backwards to understand how it came about

I asked Stephen Casper, one of the paper’s co-authors, whether artificial intelligence creates new catastrophic capabilities or simply makes existing malice easier, faster, or cheaper. “It’s more the latter,” he told me

Specifically, AI models that possess information about dangerous capabilities, such as how to disrupt infrastructure and construct a chemical weapon, could allow malicious actors to use them to nefarious ends

title: A Very Suspicious Prosecution of Two Former FBI Officials
excerpt: Not too long ago, the Department of Justice could generally be trusted to prosecute cases in which lawyers believed that real wrongdoing had occurred
body: Not too long ago, the Department of Justice could generally be trusted to prosecute cases in which lawyers believed that real wrongdoing had occurred
Now DOJ frequently unveils lawsuits that seem designed mostly for securing likes and reposts on right-wing social media—the actual facts be damned
Any high-profile criminal case brought by the Trump administration arrives with an air of suspicion

Today, Jeanine Pirro, the top federal prosecutor for Washington, D.C., announced an odd set of charges against two former FBI officials for allegedly lying to Congress during testimony in 2023. “When senior FBI agents lie to Congress believing they are above the law, it’s time to bring the hammer of justice down on them,” Pirro posted on X
For all of the fanfare, DOJ provided little evidence to back up its claims

But the timing of the charges—they’ve arrived just more than a week before the midterm elections—and with the puzzling substance of the allegations and the administration’s crowing online, does not inspire confidence in the integrity of the prosecutorial work

The charges concern several statements made by the defendants, Nikki Floris and Bradley Benavides, in the course of a congressional investigation into supposed “weaponization” of the government against President Trump
In brief, the Justice Department is alleging that Floris and Benavides lied to the House Judiciary Committee regarding their level of knowledge about the FBI’s handling of Hunter Biden’s laptop

Lawyers for Floris issued a statement saying that DOJ “has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts.” Benavides’s lawyer likewise described the charges as “baseless.” The saga of the Hunter Biden laptop has now spanned four federal elections, and the specifics of the story may, reasonably, no longer be top of mind
Understanding its relevance here requires a deep plunge into far-right mythology

But the quick version is that MAGA became obsessed with the possibly stolen laptop, and the material it contained documenting Biden’s drug addiction, after the New York Post published an article about the laptop in the lead-up to the 2020 election

Social-media companies, burned by their experience of Russian election interference in 2016, worried that the underlying documents might be Russian misinformation. (This suspicion was never confirmed.) They responded aggressively by suppressing links to the Post ’s story—which outraged the right

The laptop would go on to play a starring role in the coming years as the GOP used congressional investigations to tell a story about the victimization of the right, supposedly having been a target of a sprawling network of government-backed online censorship and unfair treatment by the FBI
This was the context in which Floris and Benavides were testifying in 2023
The two had held leadership positions in the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force (FITF) during 2020, a section created to respond to foreign interference after Russia’s 2016 election meddling
There they had crossed paths with the laptop

In recent years, congressional Republicans have pointed to various decontextualized snippets of that testimony and internal FBI documents as part of their efforts to suggest that the FBI was working against Trump in the 2020 election
By then, for a certain kind of very online Trump supporter, Floris and Benavides had already become familiar if relatively minor villains in the anticanon of deep-state enemies
The criminal charges today make sense in this larger narrative

In his X post announcing the charges, FBI Director Kash Patel referred to the agency’s past “political weaponization targeting their opponents.” Just because MAGA hates someone does not mean that they are innocent
But Floris and Benavides’s work as described in the affidavit seems unremarkable
And the document is opaque when describing what the two defendants are actually alleged to have lied about

To be prosecutable under the relevant statute, a lie to government authorities must be told “knowingly and willfully,” and it must be “material” in a way that substantively affects the investigation in question
Some of Floris’s and Benavides’s alleged misstatements, as described in the affidavit, don’t initially appear to be misstatements at all

For example, Floris said she was not involved in the criminal investigation into Hunter Biden during which the FBI seized the laptop; in fact, her work at the FITF really was separate from the criminal probe, which was carried out by a different team
Other supposed lies might well be better understood as forgetfulness
The two defendants were high up in the bureau and wouldn’t necessarily recall the minutiae of an incident that took place three years before they testified

In one instance, the affidavit alleges that Floris lied about her involvement in “an assessment to discredit the Hunter Biden investigations,” but contains no further mention of this supposed assessment nor any quotes from the relevant testimony
Perhaps DOJ will be able to provide more evidence for its allegations as the case goes on, but as things now stand, the charges appear less than airtight
How the Justice Department chose to bring this case also invites suspicion

The charges were filed via a criminal complaint, a method the government uses in many investigations that must move quickly, because a complaint does not require the immediate involvement of a grand jury
The need to rush here is hard to see, given that the relevant testimony was three years ago

Conversely, it’s easy to imagine why DOJ would want to push out incendiary allegations without having to convince a potentially skeptical grand jury—an all-but-certainty in D.C., where jurors have delivered a number of high-profile rebuttals to federal prosecutors
In the next 30 days, if the department wishes to move forward with the case, it will have to seek a grand jury’s indictment
By then, though, the Trump administration may have already gotten the propaganda boost it was looking for

At a hearing today, Magistrate Judge Zia Faruqui appeared skeptical of the case, noting the government’s decision to delay seeking an indictment and describing the defendants’ “sparkling backgrounds.” As many judges have commented over the past year, the traditional “presumption of regularity” awarded to the Justice Department’s work has been eroded by the Trump administration’s habitual use of criminal prosecutions as a tool to harass the president’s enemies
With this case, DOJ has provided little material to reassure its critics.

title: The one thing everyone can do to fight for free and fair elections
excerpt: It’s an anxious moment for American voters: Will we have a free and fair election — or not? | Spencer Platt/Getty Images Election Day is almost here — but even
body: It’s an anxious moment for American voters: Will we have a free and fair election — or not? | Spencer Platt/Getty Images Election Day is almost here — but even after the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, the election won’t really be over
The vote count will take days or even weeks in some states

President Donald Trump seems certain to raise objections to results he doesn’t like — he’s already getting started in Alaska — and he has threatened to marshal the forces of the federal government in his efforts

It’s an anxious moment for American voters: Will we have a free and fair election — or not? Luckily, says Eliza Sweren-Becker, deputy director in the Brennan Center’s Voting Rights and Elections Program, there is still one thing that every American 18 and older can do to make sure their voice is heard: vote. “I think that is the intent
It’s to create a lack of confidence

It’s to discourage voters from participating,” Sweren-Becker told Vox’s Astead Herndon on America, Actually . “But the only way that that campaign to undermine our confidence and to sow distrust actually works is if voters stay home

The way to defeat that attempt to shake voters’ trust in democracy is just to participate.” Sweren-Becker spoke with Astead about what states could do to speed up their vote counts and ensure everyone has a chance to cast their ballot, the need to restore the Voting Rights Act, and the long-term impact of Trump’s election denialism
Below is an excerpt of their conversation, edited for length and clarity
There’s much more in the full show, so listen to America, Actually wherever you get your podcasts or watch it on Vox’s YouTube channel
More than a dozen states count late-arriving ballots
President Donald Trump has used the shifting vote counts as pretense to further his own election interference claims

How prepared should folks be for a long wait in November for results? And how that could impact confidence in the results? You’re absolutely right that we may get results out of states or in certain races in the days following Election Day
Voters should not expect to have the final result on Election Day
And when you hear reporting on the news that somebody’s ahead or somebody’s behind, remember: They haven’t counted all the votes yet
The critical thing is we need to count every vote, and every person’s vote needs to be counted
So while it is true that some states allow ballots to arrive after Election Day, they all have to be cast by Election Day
The Supreme Court just this year said that it’s totally appropriate for states to set their own ballot receipt deadlines
We have to be patient, as an American electorate, to get the proper results to count every ballot and make sure all the voices are heard

But isn’t it kinda wild that we can’t get results on election night? I saw Donald Trump cite the Brazilian presidential election, and while I know he’s doing that from a self-interested place, I did think for a second: Why does it take so long for us to put these results together? I could totally understand why people would prefer the results faster
And candidly, could states do better at preparing and counting faster? Sure
They are working their butts off to prepare for the election with the staff that they have, and then they work tremendously hard to count properly, accurately, as fast as they can
Could states change their policies to allow them, in some places, to pre-process ballots, to allow them to get to results faster? Sure
I’m not saying states shouldn’t change their policies to create more efficiency here
But given the rules of the road that we have, we need to make sure that every properly cast ballot is counted
If I’m someone who is concerned about election security and free and fair elections, what should I be looking out for? So, for example, I have heard that there is some anxiety about mail voting
If you want to cast a mail ballot, just know that you probably have a bunch of options in your state as to how you can cast it
You can certainly rely on the mail and have USPS deliver that ballot, but of course, we know occasionally mail gets delayed
You may have ballot drop-off at election officials’ offices, or even at polling places
Voters should also check their voter registration status
Make sure it’s up to date with their current address
Of course, if you’re not registered to vote and you still have time in your state to register, please do register
Our democracy works best the more of us that can participate
If your registration date has not passed, don’t forget to register to vote
Vote with your friends, vote with your community, vote with your family
It’s a civic experience that I think is really fun
I try to take my kids with me to vote because it’s exciting
You get your sticker, other people see you, they know it’s Election Day, maybe they go out to vote
It’s a way to be part of your community and invest in your community and to choose who you want to be a leader of your community

What about after Election Day? Earlier this year, Democrats and Republicans in Congress circulated a letter asking members to commit to recognizing state-certified winners and “oppose any attempt to refuse or delay a seating of a member-elect.” We saw House Speaker Mike Johnson delay the swearing-in of an Arizona representative last year, That seems to me like maybe a preview of what might be to come
How fearful should we be of these post-election attempts to block members from being seated? I think those scenarios are highly unlikely

title: A truck full of cows crashed in Kansas City. It reveals a bigger everyday horror.
excerpt: Cows on the loose in Kansas City, October 18. | Vox; Video still from u/airitek on Reddit Very often, a viral news story about animals is a comedy to its audien
body: Cows on the loose in Kansas City, October 18. | Vox; Video still from u/airitek on Reddit Very often, a viral news story about animals is a comedy to its audience and an unmitigated tragedy to its subjects

That was the case this past weekend, as footage of bands of juvenile cows dashing through the streets of Kansas City stampeded across the internet.  The details are as follows: Last weekend, in the middle of the night, a semitruck carrying close to 120 young cattle plunged off a highway interchange in Kansas City’s downtown, spilling out dozens of animals
The truck driver and one other person sustained minor injuries
Dozens of the cows were killed, many others were seriously injured, and still others went running into the city
Some of them traveled for several miles, the city’s fire chief told the Associated Press

The animals were chased around the streets by first responders and self-described “cowboys” (one of them appearing to carry an electric cord as a lasso); authorities said all were rounded up by the end of the day

To many people, freak accidents like these understandably look a little funny, even fantastical. “We take free roam BBQ very seriously,” one Reddit comment , with more than 400 upvotes as of this writing, said. “Much as I lament the tragic loss of bovine life, these videos have brought such joy to our fair city,” another commenter wrote .  The clips undoubtedly have a certain charm
If only the animals were as carefree as they appeared in those brief moments — and if only they could truly escape the fate that humans had in store for them

But as my colleague Kenny Torrella has written , the strange animal stories that periodically capture the public’s imagination almost invariably circulate stripped of the darker reality from which they emerge — humanity’s dominion over nonhuman animals

In this case, the cattle crash illuminates one of the most overlooked cruelties of modern animal agriculture: the nightmare of livestock transportation.   When you imagine the lives of animals raised for food, you might think of a factory farm (in a large majority of cases , very cruel) or a slaughterhouse (likewise, and not just for animals raised primarily for meat — dairy cows and egg-laying hens are slaughtered, too)

But the animals need to be transported from the farm to the slaughterhouse, and also between numerous different facilities — breeding farms, hatcheries, feedlots, auctions — over the course of their lives as they progress through different stages of the livestock supply chain
Most cattle raised for beef and dairy are transported multiple times in their lifetimes; between four and six journeys is common
A recent US Department of Agriculture report found that half of cattle shipped to feedlots traveled for more than 250 miles, and 22 percent traveled more than 500 miles
Louis, and Omaha, Nebraska, was once a major national hub of livestock transportation, with cattle arriving by the trainload at its busy stockyards (earning the city its nickname, “cowtown”)

But the rail-based livestock trade that made it famous has largely vanished, replaced by a sprawling system of truck transit that carry animals between farms, feedlots, and slaughterhouses across the country

These form the connective tissue that makes it possible for the American livestock industry to raise and slaughter nearly 10 billion land animals every year.  You’ve probably seen livestock trucks on the interstate, with their long, aluminum bodies and oval ventilation holes
They appear unremarkable enough from the outside
But the most important thing to understand about farm animal transportation is that these creatures are not handled like passengers, the way you or I would be treated on a long-distance trip
Rather, they are freight, loaded into metal trailers, often packed tightly together  for long, very uncomfortable, sometimes dangerous stretches of highway travel

Picture yourself hurtling down the interstate in a box at 70 miles an hour, struggling to balance for many hours, without a seat, a seat belt, heating or cooling, or any of the other protections designed to keep human passengers safe and comfortable
As the hours pass, urine and manure accumulate beneath the animals’ feet, which can cause them to slip

The trips “can span many hours and thousands of miles, potentially exposing livestock to overcrowding, extreme temperatures, limited ventilation, and lack of access to water or food, among other things,” according to a damning report on farm animal transportation released over the summer by the US Government Accountability Office (GAO). “If not managed properly, these conditions can lead to injury, illness, or death.”  Even the process by which animals are herded onto the trucks is often highly stressful , with frightened animals pushed, prodded, pulled, and otherwise handled roughly

I have reviewed, over the years, more videos than I can count of stressed farmworkers treating cows and pigs in ways that appear appalling to people not steeped in animal agriculture, simply because they’re desperate to meet the demands of their jobs and get the animals to move
According to a 2022 investigation by The Guardian, more than 20 million animals every year “are dead on arrival, or soon after,” when they reach a slaughterhouse

Most of those are chickens , the species that makes up the overwhelming majority of land animals raised for food; about 166,000 of them, per The Guardian, were cattle.  Catastrophic crashes like what happened in Kansas City are far rarer than the more routine, mundane cruelties of livestock transportation, but they do happen regularly
On a cursory search, I was able to find 20 others that have occurred in the US so far this year

Aaron Caster, who owns the towing company that handled the recovery operation in the crash, told me that almost all of the animals were female, and estimated they were around 6 months old, not yet fully grown
They’d been shipped from Virginia, he said, and had been on their way to Nebraska
Caster’s account of the scene of the crash is harrowing. “The cab was ripped off the truck, the trailer was on its side with the entire trailer blown apart,” he told me. “Just cows everywhere
Some alive, some were dead.” Some had “really busted legs, ripped up pretty good,” and were euthanized
Caster, who is also a rancher, said he took more than 50 surviving cows to his property in Bates City, Missouri, to recover
Two of those have since died, he told me earlier this week, including one who had been “cut up pretty bad” in the crash and was euthanized after developing an infection

In the US, there’s one major law designed to protect the well-being of livestock animals in transit: The Twenty-Eight-Hour Law of 1873, which says that livestock in transit traveling across state lines can’t be confined for more than 28 hours without being unloaded for rest, food, and water.  That rule excludes poultry birds entirely, meaning that the vast majority of animals raised for food aren’t covered — a major oversight
But even for those species that nominally benefit from it, the law is very rarely enforced
Farmed animal advocacy groups have documented and complained about that for years, and the GAO this summer similarly reported that enforcement is extremely limited

The report paints a picture of the federal system for protecting farm animals in transit as woefully inadequate and largely toothless, dating back to the era when livestock traveled primarily by rail.  The report identified six factors that contribute to cruel conditions for animals on the road, including not just the length of the trip but also temperature extremes, unsafe and unsanitary vehicles, rough handling, and being transported when they’re too sick, injured, or vulnerable (like animals who are extremely young or heavily pregnant)

Federal law fails to cover most of those dangers while offering almost no meaningful enforcement of the 28-hour duration rule that is in place.  Between 2013 and 2025, the USDA investigated just 23 suspected violations of the law, resulting in no fines and only four warning letters — and in 2022, the GAO report notes, the USDA stopped issuing even those

The GAO contrasts the US system with more modernized protections in Canada, Mexico, Australia, and the European Union, which include requirements around animals’ fitness for travel, adequate space, humane handling, and vehicle safety

Some of the most heartbreaking livestock transportation conditions that I’ve personally covered have been in the dairy industry , where it’s common to ship fragile newborn calves, just separated from their mothers, across long distances
It’s also routine to ship dairy cows on long journeys to slaughter once they’re no longer profitable

title: Trump is trying to overturn an election that hasn’t happened yet
excerpt: Mary Peltola, a Democratic from Alaska and US Senate candidate, speaks during the 2026 Alaska Fisheries Debate with Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican from Alas
body: Mary Peltola, a Democratic from Alaska and US Senate candidate, speaks during the 2026 Alaska Fisheries Debate with Senator Dan Sullivan, a Republican from Alaska, not pictured, in Kodiak, Alaska, on September 12, 2026. | Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images President Donald Trump’s Justice Department filed a lawsuit on Thursday seeking to block former Democratic Rep
Mary Peltola’s victory in the 2026 US Senate election
If you’re confused by this development, you should be
Because the election won’t happen for more than a week
The case arises out of an odd candidacy that might undercut incumbent Republican Sen
Sullivan’s reelection bid against Peltola

Sullivan also secured a spot on the ballot, and Republicans fear that the not -Senator Sullivan’s presence on the ballot might trick voters who wish to vote for the incumbent into voting for the not-senator instead
But there are two reasons to doubt that not-Senator Sullivan will attract many voters who actually wanted to vote for the Republican
According to a sample ballot published by Alaska’s Division of Elections, Sen

Sullivan will be identified as a “Registered Republican” and as the “Incumbent,” so voters will be told which Dan Sullivan to vote for if they wish to reelect the one who is actually a senator.  Additionally, Alaska uses ranked-choice voting , a system where voters rank candidates in order of preference, and votes cast for losing candidates are redistributed to voters’ next choice

So an Alaska voter who wants to reelect the Dan Sullivan who is actually a senator, but who is confused as to which Dan Sullivan is the incumbent, can simply rank both Dans Sullivan as their top two choices, and the ranked choice system should ensure that their vote is counted as a vote for Senator Sullivan (and against Peltola)
The question of whether not-Senator Sullivan may appear on the ballot, moreover, has already been litigated

Initially, the Alaska Division of Elections, which is led by a Republican , attempted to disqualify the not-senator because it concluded that he did not seek election to the Senate in “good faith.” Not-Senator Sullivan sued, and an Alaska court ordered him reinstated as a candidate because “the Division’s decision to exclude Mr
Sullivan from the primary ballot was based on a ‘good-faith’ requirement that does not appear in the U.S

Constitution, the Alaska Statutes, or the implementing regulations adopted by the Division” — that is, there is not actually a law that prevents the not-senator from running, even if he is intentionally running as a spoiler candidate
This lower court order was affirmed by the Alaska Supreme Court last June
If Republicans thought that this decision violates federal law, they could have asked the Division of Elections — which, again, is run by a Republican — to appeal to the US Supreme Court

Instead, they appear to have let the issue lie until less than two weeks before Election Day, when Trump’s Justice Department filed a new, federal lawsuit claiming that not-Senator Sullivan’s presence on the ballot is somehow illegal, and asking a federal court to preemptively block a Peltola victory in the upcoming election
Trump says that he personally told the Justice Department to file this suit
It is difficult to find an actual legal argument, much less a persuasive one, anywhere in the Trump DOJ’s complaint initiating the lawsuit

Trump’s lawsuit also runs afoul of something called the “ Purcell principle” — a concept that, ironically, the Supreme Court reaffirmed the same day that the Trump administration filed its suit — which says that federal courts should be reluctant to intervene in election-related disputes when the election itself is about to happen
It is likely, in other words, that the Trump administration’s attempt to overturn a Democratic victory that hasn’t even happened yet will fail
But the mere existence of this new lawsuit, which is known as United States v
Alaska , is an ominous sign that the Trump administration will use every tool in its shed to overturn Democratic victories in the upcoming election

So what are the actual legal arguments in the Alaska case? It is a bit of a stretch to even describe the Justice Department’s complaint in this case as a “legal” document, as the complaint does not so much as point to any law that either not-Senator Sullivan or the state of Alaska may have violated, and instead vaguely alludes to legal sources that use terms like “integrity.” Specifically, the Justice Department points to a federal law which says that it has four purposes, one of which is to “ protect the integrity of the electoral process .” It also points to the Supreme Court’s decision in Bullock v

Carter (1972), which said that “a State has an interest, if not a duty, to protect the integrity of its political processes from frivolous or fraudulent candidacies.” But the statute that Trump’s lawyers quote, the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 , does not concern which candidates’ names should appear on the ballot
As its name suggests, it is a law about voter registration, and it imposes requirements on states, such as requiring them to register voters when those voters obtain a driver’s license

Similarly, while Bullock does include a single line indicating that states may enact laws targeting “frivolous or fraudulent candidacies,” nothing in the opinion suggests that sharing another candidate’s name makes someone’s candidacy frivolous or fraudulent

The decision itself concerned unusually high fees charged to a candidate for public office in Texas, and the Court concluded that Texas’s fees were unconstitutional.  The line about “frivolous or fraudulent candidacies,” meanwhile, was included to clarify that states still have some power to regulate ballot access

While Bullock concluded that Texas’s fees were excessive, the opinion also suggests that states may impose more reasonable filing fees on candidates to discourage unserious candidates from seeking office
Alaska, for example, charges a modest filing fee of $100 to US Senate candidates

The Trump DOJ’s entire argument, in other words, appears to turn on the fact that it identified two legal sources that use the word “integrity” in contexts that bear little resemblance to the Alaska case.  Nevertheless, Trump’s lawyers claim that the court must prevent Alaska from certifying a Peltola victory “pending an investigation to determine whether votes cast for Daniel J

Sullivan were meant to be cast for Senator Sullivan.” This lawsuit also cannot be squared with one of the Republican Party’s favorite legal doctrines Even if Trump’s Justice Department had a persuasive argument that leaving not-Senator Sullivan on the ballot is illegal, they should still lose Alaska because they waited too long to file the case

Gonzalez (2006), the Supreme Court warned that “court orders affecting elections, especially conflicting orders, can themselves result in voter confusion and consequent incentive to remain away from the polls,” and it added that this “risk will increase” as Election Day draws closer

More recent decisions, many of them joined only by the Court’s Republicans, have read this “ Purcell principle” quite expansively to forbid federal courts from issuing election-related decisions in the months leading up to an election
Justice Brett Kavanaugh has even claimed that Purcell prevents federal courts from issuing election-related decisions as soon as nine months before the general election date
Supreme Court decisions invoking Purcell to shut down lower court orders altering a state’s election rules are now very common in the weeks leading up to an election
On Thursday, for example, the Court relied on the Purcell principle to block a lower court order that would have made it easier for college students to vote in New Hampshire

The Court began its decision with this line: “This Court has repeatedly emphasized that lower federal courts should ordinarily not alter the election rules on the eve of an election.”  Trump’s DOJ, meanwhile, did not even file its lawsuit seeking to preemptively invalidate a Peltola victory until less than two weeks before Election Day
If Purcell means anything, it must mean that a federal court cannot force Alaska to kick a candidate off the ballot mere days before a federal election.

title: The GOP’s Midterms-Money Advantage Has Its Limits
excerpt: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the
body: This is an edition of The Atlantic Daily, a newsletter that guides you through the biggest stories of the day, helps you discover new ideas, and recommends the best in culture
American politics is saturated with cash, and each election cycle seems to set new spending records—and yet, with the midterms in the home stretch, neither party thinks it has enough money
The irony is nearly as rich as the biggest donors
Filings released this week show that $1 billion was spent on the campaign in the first two weeks of October alone
This year’s elections are expected to be the most expensive midterms in U.S. history, beating 2022 —which beat 2018, which beat 2014, and so on

This will not surprise anyone who lives in a state or district with a competitive race this fall. (I’m sure I can still recite the Senate Leadership Fund’s ad attacking the North Carolina Democrat Roy Cooper, weeks after it stopped running .) Democratic and Republican voters don’t agree on a ton these days, but they’re united on one position: There’s too much money in politics
Ask officials and candidates in both parties, though, and you’ll hear that they don’t have nearly enough
Democrats are feeling fairly confident about capturing the House and are getting more hopeful about their chances at winning the Senate, yet officials worry they don’t have enough cash

The party got a big boost on Monday, when Michael Bloomberg, the billionaire former New York mayor and presidential candidate, announced that he would pour $80 million into helping Democrats before Election Day
Republicans came into this election with a huge money advantage, and they continue to have millions available to spend
Even so, major GOP organizations are finding themselves having to make unpleasant choices to stop spending in races that seem to be slipping away from them

Senate Leadership Fund, which is the top Republican PAC supporting Senate races, didn’t spend any money on TV ads last week to support the Georgia candidate Mike Collins , who is expected to lose to Senator Jon Ossoff

SLF had already pulled back from helping the Republican Senate candidate Michael Whatley in North Carolina. (To make matters worse, President Trump hosted a rally with Whatley on Tuesday in Greenville, where he said that Cooper is “going to become your senator, and it’s crazy.”) One reason both parties are scrambling for money is that the map has shifted
As Trump’s political position deteriorates and he drags GOP candidates along with him, races that once seemed like foregone conclusions are now real battles
Democrats worry that they don’t have enough funding to match their potential
Republicans, by contrast, are having to play defense in what they thought were safe seats
SLF has moved money from North Carolina to Kansas, a state where a Democrat hasn’t won a Senate race since 1932 but where Adam Hamilton is posing a real threat to Senator Roger Marshall

Republicans are also finding that their decision to squeeze new gerrymanders out of some states before this election has been costly: Districts that they expected to be easy Republican pickups are now close combat

Punchbowl News recently reported that although the GOP has a lock on five of 14 new districts, “Republican candidates and super PACs have spent nearly $100 million on ads trying to flip the other nine districts” since September 1
Another reason is that not all money is created equal
Some Democratic candidates are very well funded

The Texas Senate candidate James Talarico, for example, raised $64 million in the third quarter of the year alone—the highest total for any candidate in that period ever. (Because Texas has so many voters and so many media markets, it’s an expensive place to campaign.) But Democratic committees, including top PACs, are much more strapped

This is partly because the sitting president’s party always has a leg up in fundraising, but it’s also because many donors have grown disillusioned with the Democratic Party, upset with strategic decisions in the 2024 presidential loss, chaotic management of the Democratic National Committee since, and uninspiring leadership by elected officials
Republican candidates (such as Talarico’s opponent, Ken Paxton) have relatively little money on hand, but committees and PACs are still flush
Much of that money comes from independent-expenditure groups, such as super PACs
An analysis by the Brennan Center for Justice finds that these groups spent $2 billion through the end of September, leaning heavily toward Republicans
The single largest donor is Elon Musk, who has spent $366 million this cycle alone
But one disadvantage of independent-expenditure groups is that they have to pay higher rates for advertisements than candidates
That’s perhaps the dominant theme of the late campaign: Republicans have lots of money, but they’re not necessarily getting much bang for their buck
At this stage in the campaign, the time to build serious infrastructure, such as canvassing operations, is past
Money can buy a lot of advertising, but TV time is either booked up or more expensive
Besides, Republicans have already spent lavishly to fill airwaves, websites, and mailboxes with ads
So far , they don’t seem to be seeing much impact : Races either remain close or appear to be shifting even further toward Democrats
Understanding why the GOP candidates are stalled is not difficult

Voters are upset about high prices, especially for fuel, and they are turned off by a president who is dismissive of their affordability concerns, distracted by vanity projects, and bogged down in an unpopular and inflationary war in Iran
Trump’s super PAC has $164 million left to spend , but as any orthodox Lennonist knows, money can’t buy you love
Related: Small-dollar campaign donors are hurting the political system

The agreement, brokered with help from First Lady Melania Trump and Pope Leo XIV, will allow humanitarian aid to enter the city and civilians to evacuate amid a worsening food crisis

title: The Download: testing six tech promises and biotech’s blind spots

body: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology
Are we there yet? A reality check on six big tech promises Some seemingly impossible feats are too good to give up on
Decoding a pet’s yowls and yips? Absolutely
Scrubbing the world of forever chemicals? Yes, please

Rocketing to Mars in a fraction of the time? Sounds great, but how close are we, really? In the new Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review , we ran progress reports on six potentially transformative technologies and ideas that have been “just around the corner” for years, or even decades
From exercise in a pill to nuclear-powered spaceships, we asked experts what’s holding them back and how far they’ve come
Check out our stories on how they all stacked up
Over the coming days, we’ll unpack each of the six technologies in The Download

So stay tuned! In the biotech world, you can’t see everything —Jessica Hamzelou Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything , the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.  Like many others, I came away feeling unsettled
But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the disturbing interactions between the subjects
The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything
The film is a stark reminder of how easy it can be to fall for an appealing narrative
This is why it left me questioning how we cover science
This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter

Now, some researchers are trying something different: listening to the universe

Using sonification, the process of turning information into sound, they’re helping blind and visually impaired researchers explore the cosmos—and even uncover patterns that might otherwise go unnoticed
The approach is spreading beyond astronomy into fields like climate science, navigation, and education
Discover how sound could make science more accessible—and even more revealing . —Corey S

title: In the biotech world, you can’t see everything
excerpt: Holmes's charm is still unsettling on screen: Even knowing the full Theranos story, the documentary captures how effectively Holmes plants seeds of doubt—j
body: Holmes's charm is still unsettling on screen: Even knowing the full Theranos story, the documentary captures how effectively Holmes plants seeds of doubt—journalists who interviewed her in her prime later admitted she had fooled them completely

Peer review isn't a perfect safety net: Science's built-in fact-checking system has real cracks—10,000 papers were retracted in 2023 alone, and preprint servers, press releases, and social media now routinely bypass it

Reporters face the same vulnerability as investors: Even seasoned science journalists rely on trust and expert opinion to vet claims, raising an uncomfortable question: how confident can anyone really be that they wouldn't have fallen for it too " data-chronoton-post-id="1147610" data-chronoton-expand-collapse="1" data-chronoton-analytics-enabled="1"> Earlier this week, I attended a screening of You Can See Everything , the buzzy new documentary about the disgraced former biotech CEO Elizabeth Holmes.  I went in not really knowing what to expect
I’d avoided spoilers (and won’t be giving anything away here, either!)

I was wondering what new information this film could reveal, given how familiar many of us are with the Theranos story thanks to years of media coverage, the best-selling book Bad Blood , and the Hulu series The Dropout , starring Amanda Seyfried
Like many others who have seen the film, I came away feeling unsettled
But not just about Holmes’s fraud and the somewhat disturbing interactions between the subjects
The film reignited a concern I’ve had about covering science for most of my career: Despite our best efforts, we never can actually see everything
In case you’re rusty on the details, Elizabeth Holmes dropped out of Stanford University in 2003 to run Theranos, a diagnostics company she founded, when she was just 19
She went on to claim that her company had invented a way to run over 100 diagnostic tests on just a few drops of blood
Holmes raised hundreds of millions of dollars for Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion in 2014
Forbes named her the youngest self-made female billionaire—she was worth $4.5 billion when she was just 30 years old
Things started to unravel in 2015, when an investigation by the Wall Street Journal raised concerns by former Theranos employees that the tests didn’t work
Some also said that the company’s device had not been tested properly, and that blood samples had been analyzed on machines from other companies instead
MIT Technology Review named it one of the biggest technology failures of 2015
Forbes had revised Holmes’s worth to $0 by 2016
That year, a damning government report said that the company’s lab was struggling with basic procedures and gave patients results even when they knew they could be wrong
In 2018, Theranos, Holmes, and former company president Ramesh Balwani were charged with “massive fraud.” In 2022, she was sentenced to a little over 11 years in prison for defrauding investors
She began serving her sentence in May 2023
It was around a month before this that filmmakers Nathan Fielder, Lance Oppenheim, and their colleagues began documenting Holmes and her partner, Billy Evans, at home with their two young children
I’m not giving anything away when I say it’s an extremely intimate portrayal—at least of how the two adults interact with Fielder, who is also a central character in the film
As you might know if you’ve seen the trailer , there are plenty of super close-ups
I felt as if I spent most of the film staring straight into the faces of those people
And almost the whole way through, they all seemed to be trying to figure each other out
Holmes is known for her dishonesty, but she invited cameras into her home in an apparent bid to reframe the narrative and position herself as an honest person with an unusual mind
Will anyone believe her? I couldn’t help feeling some empathy for Holmes, a mother we see preparing to leave her two kids for a lengthy prison sentence
And even though I have long known the facts, Holmes is clearly an effective manipulator
You can see her plant the seeds of doubt in Fielder’s mind
At times, I felt she was convincing me, sitting in my cinema seat

Maybe she really didn’t mean to lie? But then I remembered how other journalists felt after being taken in by her claims. “I blew it,” Fortune ’s Roger Parloff reflected in 2015, a year after profiling Holmes and her company. “I’m pretty sure she lied to me,” STAT ’s Matthew Herper wrote recently, having interviewed Holmes in 2015

Even the former employee turned whistleblower Tyler Shultz, who knew the product didn’t work, said that he could “have a five-minute conversation with her and walk away feeling like my work was changing the world,” he said in 2022
If I’d interviewed Holmes, would I have fallen for it all? One of the early red flags in the Theranos case was the lack of published, peer-reviewed data

Much of the company’s work was classified as a “trade secret.” Scientists tend to publish their work in journals—a slow process that involves having the work evaluated by often anonymous experts in the field, who provide feedback, highlight questionable conclusions, and often ask for clarification
Peer review is meant to add rigor to the publication process
You should be able to trust published scientific papers
Some will exaggerate their results or inflate their importance
Some manipulate data to serve a hypothesis
Sometimes these infractions are caught during peer review, but not always
There are plenty of examples of scientific findings that could never be replicated by other labs and ended up collapsing under the weight of real evidence
Many papers ultimately end up with corrections

    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767989/original/file-20261023-50-sq3v22.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C0%2C3999%2C2666&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Halloween is an opportunity for children to explore the balance between excitement and fear. </span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/houses-in-celebration-florida-get-ready-for-halloween-with-news-photo/2243800880?phrase=halloween%20scary%20decorations%20&amp;adppopup=true">Ronaldo Silva/NurPhoto via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Halloween is one of the few holidays centered around children. When else can students come to school dressed like astronauts, monsters and witches, or ring strangers’ doorbells to ask for candy? </p>

<p>But of course there’s a darker side to the holiday. </p>

<p>Horror’s bloody images lurk in the shadows – from ghouls leering over people’s lawns to skeletons hanging from trees – whether invited or not. Thoughtful adults might wonder, what is the right amount of scary for a child?</p>

<p>As a <a href="https://www.binghamton.edu/news/story/5892/book-talk-with-liz-rosenberg">professor of children’s literature, and a writer of children’s books</a>, I turn to the great author and illustrator <a href="https://www.mauricesendak.com/">Maurice Sendak</a> for a hint.</p>

<p>A child’s mother once told Sendak that her pre-schooler was terrified of his classic 1963 book “<a href="https://archive.org/details/wherewildthingsa0000unse_t5p2/page/n7/mode/2up">Where the Wild Things Are</a>,” which brings the reader into the world of an imaginative child, Max, after his mother sends him to his room without dinner. Through his imagination, Max journeys to a world of fantastical creatures called Wild Things. </p>

<p>No matter how many times this mother read “Where the Wild Things Are” to her young child, he screamed.</p>

<p>“What are you, a sadist?” Sendak answered. “Read him something else.”</p>

<p>“Why,” he continued, “<a href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=2p5an0w4XWs">would any one book be right for every child</a>?” </p>

<p>When considering the benefits and drawbacks of scary books to get in the spirit of Halloween, some possible choices come to mind, along with some reminders to both overly cautious and sometimes careless adults.</p>

<h2>Facing your jitters head on</h2>

<p>To start, Felicia Bond’s 1987 “<a href="https://feliciabond.brandyourself.com/">The Halloween Performance</a>,” later republished as “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/the-halloween-play-felicia-bond?variant=32117649899554">The Halloween Play</a>,” is a perfect Halloween picture-book classic, appealing to all ages and offering humor and suspense. </p>

<p>Bond is the illustrator of the 1985 children’s best seller, “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/pages/mouse-cookie-books">If You Give a Mouse a Cookie</a>,” and subsequent books. An adorable young mouse features in this Halloween story, as well. </p>

<p>The plot revolves around a mysterious “small but important part” that Roger, a nervous, brown mouse, has landed in the school Halloween performance. </p>

<p>Costumed skeletons and witches don’t bother him – but his jitters about performing on stage do. </p>

<p>Roger overcomes stage-fright to shine in the school performance. He may inspire other children to overcome their own feelings of nervousness at Halloween and make fun memories. </p>

<h2>Frog and Toad show that fear can be fun</h2>

<p>Frog and Toad are Arnold Lobel’s <a href="https://www.icanread.com/books/9780062983428/frog-and-toad-a-complete-reading-collection/">beloved, amphibian best friends</a> from his children’s series published in the 1970s. </p>

<p>Though they have very different personalities, both Frog and Toad enjoy the thrill of playing with fear. In “<a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/days-with-frog-and-toad-arnold-lobel?variant=44772245012514">Shivers</a>,” a story in the book “Days with Frog and Toad,” Frog tells Toad a tale about “the old dark Frog” who combs the woods in search of tasty children. </p>

<p>Toad keeps asking, “Is this real?” Frog answers like any good storyteller, “Maybe it is and maybe it isn’t.”</p>

<p>Together the duo enjoy scaring themselves into a teeth-chattering but delightful evening. </p>

<p>They show young readers that, in the right doses, fear can be fun: ask any kid scream-laughing on a roller-coaster.</p>

<p>In another story, “<a href="https://www.prindleinstitute.org/books/dragons-and-giants-from-frog-and-toad-together/">Dragons and Giants</a>,” Frog and Toad test their own heroism after reading fairy tales about dragons and giants. </p>

<blockquote>“The people in this book are brave,” said Toad. <br> “They fight dragons and giants, and they are never afraid.” </blockquote> 

<blockquote>“I wonder if we are brave,” said Frog. <br> Frog and Toad looked into a mirror. “We look brave,” said Frog. “Yes, but are we?” asked Toad.</blockquote> 

<p>Frog and Toad are both fearful and brave, as most of us are. </p>

<p>Wise children’s stories reinforce the truth that it’s natural to be both, sometimes at the same time. “Frog and Toad” features color illustrations in subtle greens and browns, leaving enough space for kids to imagine new facets of themselves – the timid and the bold.</p>

<h2>Scary stories can be a natural part of childhood</h2>

<p>Fear is inevitably woven into the fabric of children’s lives. </p>

<p>Nightmares, for example, spring from unknown sources, though studies show they are intensified by <a href="https://www.psychologytoday.com/us/blog/sleep-newzzz/201107/tv-nightmares-and-childrens-sleep">trauma, emotional disturbances and exposure to violence</a>. </p>

<p>Bad dreams – like scary stories – work as fire drills for the developing brain.</p>

<p>“Bad dreams may even provide evolutionary protection for the young, by allowing children to practice bravery while they are safely at home and in bed,” writes Dierdre Barrett, editor of the book “<a href="https://www.hup.harvard.edu/books/9780674006904">Traumas and Dreams</a>.” She notes that children are smaller and more “vulnerable to many more threats than adults. Nightmares … reflect this vulnerability.”</p>

<p>Recognizing the difference between fantasy and reality is a form of practicing fear management – which strengthens resilience and resistance. </p>

<p>Maybe that’s why some older elementary school kids actively seek out frightening reading. </p>

<p>When written well and thoughtfully, such books provide more delight than dismay. The only hair-raising thing about <a href="https://www.harpercollins.com/products/scary-stories-to-tell-in-the-dark-alvin-schwartz?variant=47506500517922">Alvin Schwartz’s “Scary Stories”</a> is Stephen Gammell’s high-contrast, dreamlike art. Schwartz, a writer and folklorist, gathered spooky tales from all over the United States and compiled them into three of the most popular children’s books of the 1980s. </p>

<p>While Schwartz retells classic folklore tales with humor and goosebumps in equal measure, Gammell’s powerful drawings nudge children wordlessly toward the ghoulish. It’s a good match: The three-book series has proven irresistible to young readers for 40 years. </p>

<p>At the darkest haunting edge of the children’s horror genre, <a href="https://www.bbc.com/culture/article/20160912-the-dark-side-of-roald-dahl">books like Roald Dahl’s</a> “<a href="https://www.roalddahl.com/stories/the-witches">The Witches</a>” totter between imaginatively eerie and terror-producing. </p>

<p>In this book, ordinary-seeming women unmask themselves as grotesquely evil witches. Their goal is to capture human children, transforming them into mice that they will trap and kill.</p>

<h2>Navigating scary things, safely</h2>

<p>What constitutes protection and when does it <a href="https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3808745/">deny the child a chance to explore their fears</a>? I believe we want our children to enjoy adventures, to test themselves and discover inner courage when they least expect it. </p>

<p>We also don’t want them to be haunted for life. The right books for the right child at the right time can help children and adults safely navigate those waters.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294433/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Ancestors all around – millions of dead people linger in Americans’ memories</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767705/original/file-20261022-50-phtlmm.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=2%2C0%2C5994%2C3996&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Millions of deceased family members are gone but not forgotten by the living.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://unsplash.com/photos/scattered-vintage-black-and-white-photographs-depicting-people-and-scenes-EkZMVC_XQ-0">Wolfgang Vrede/Unsplash</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Halloween kicks off a series of religious and cultural festivals to honor the dead, including All Saints’ Day, All Souls’ Day and the Day of the Dead. But deceased loved ones don’t disappear from people’s social worlds once the ghost and skeleton decorations come down.</p>

<p>Present in memory and tradition, the <a href="https://doi.org/10.1146/annurev-soc-090324-035534">dead can shape people’s identities and behaviors</a> long after they die. Recent survey data shows that <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2023/08/23/many-americans-report-interacting-with-dead-relatives-in-dreams-or-other-ways/">almost 44% of Americans report</a> that they have felt the presence of a deceased relative or that they have communicated with a deceased relative in the past year alone.</p>

<p>Researchers lack basic knowledge about this shadow population. <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=t-47vMAAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">As demographers</a>, <a href="http://scholar.google.com/citations?user=x0hHFh8AAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">we typically study</a> the living. But in our recent work, we asked a very unusual demographic question: What does a population of our deceased relatives look like?</p>

<h2>Characterizing an unusual population</h2>

<p>Our research typically categorizes the living population by age groups and other demographic attributes. In our recent study, we took our analysis a step further to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/23780231261474337">estimate the size and age distribution</a> of the currently living population’s deceased relatives. We focused specifically on deceased grandparents, parents, siblings, spouses and children.</p>

<p>To do this project, we relied on a modeling framework called <a href="http://www.zagheni.net/uploads/3/4/4/7/34477700/microsimulation_in_demographic_research.pdf">demographic microsimulations</a>. This approach produces results only for Black and white Americans. The method cannot estimate relative populations living outside of the United States, so it excludes groups with high percentages of foreign-born individuals who have family abroad. </p>

<p>Our study focused on the populations as of July 2020, but for the purposes of this article, we updated our analysis and weighted results to the estimated population as of October 2026.</p>

<p><iframe id="ku0Ln" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/ku0Ln/5/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="Bar chart shows the number of deceased in living people's memories is much greater than the number of people currently alive"></iframe></p>

<p>Because estimating the deceased relative population is not a common exercise in our field, we had to make some modeling decisions. We counted only deceased relatives who died after the birth of at least one person still alive; if no one remains who could remember them, we did not include them.</p>

<p>Also, we counted deceased persons based on how many relatives they have in the living population. For example, if a deceased 60-year-old man is survived by a spouse, an adult child, a grandchild and a sibling, we count him in the deceased relative population four times, reflecting his being remembered by four living individuals. As such, the deceased relative population we quantified is really a count of how many direct relative ties remain to those who are dead.</p>

<p>And finally, we classified deceased relatives according to their age at death. We believe this represents the age many people will most clearly remember their deceased loved ones. Of course, we categorize the living population by their current age.</p>

<h2>Deceased relatives of today’s Americans</h2>

<p>Our results included several key findings.</p>

<p>First, the deceased relative population is large. Our model estimated that the living Black and white populat,ion <a href="https://doi.org/10.18128/D010.V16.0">representing about 217 million people</a>, had <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/23780231261474337">755 million ties to deceased close relatives</a>. That’s a population more than three times the size of the living population. For every under-15-year-old out trick-or-treating on Halloween, there are about 21 deceased relatives remembered. </p>

<p>Second, our model shows that, on average, the deceased relatives died 25 years ago. That the average deceased relative has been remembered for a quarter of a century makes it clear that loved ones are often suspended in memory for years, even decades, after their deaths. </p>

<p><iframe id="opqMj" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/opqMj/1/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="a roughly bell-shaped line graph shows years of birth along the horizontal access and millions of people along the vertical axis"></iframe></p>

<p>Third, over half of the deceased relative population was born more than 100 years ago – even before the term “trick-or-treating” <a href="https://www.wsj.com/articles/tricks-or-treats-goes-singular-1446228817">took hold in the U.S</a>. Around 10% of the deceased relatives were born before 1900, with 140,000 of them born before the Civil War – these are the remembered grandparents of today’s oldest individuals. These results speak to how generations of the seemingly long ago past still have a direct tie to the living.</p>

<p>The Halloween season reminds us of ghosts, spirits and ancestors. Whatever their beliefs, many Americans also carry relationships with people who are no longer alive: grandparents whose recipes they still make, parents whose advice they still hear, spouses whose absence shapes their days.</p>

<p>These relationships are deeply personal, but together they form a vast and previously unstudied shadow population. By quantifying and characterizing the deceased relative population, our research reveals just how many people no longer appear in the census yet remain an integral part of our social world.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292342/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />
