body: Millions of deceased family members are gone but not forgotten by the living
Wolfgang Vrede/Unsplash Halloween kicks off a series of religious and cultural festivals to honor the dead, including All Saints’ Day, All Souls’ Day and the Day of the Dead
But deceased loved ones don’t disappear from people’s social worlds once the ghost and skeleton decorations come down
Present in memory and tradition, the dead can shape people’s identities and behaviors long after they die
Recent survey data shows that almost 44% of Americans report that they have felt the presence of a deceased relative or that they have communicated with a deceased relative in the past year alone
Researchers lack basic knowledge about this shadow population
As demographers , we typically study the living

But in our recent work, we asked a very unusual demographic question: What does a population of our deceased relatives look like? Characterizing an unusual population Our research typically categorizes the living population by age groups and other demographic attributes
In our recent study, we took our analysis a step further to estimate the size and age distribution of the currently living population’s deceased relatives
We focused specifically on deceased grandparents, parents, siblings, spouses and children
To do this project, we relied on a modeling framework called demographic microsimulations
This approach produces results only for Black and white Americans
The method cannot estimate relative populations living outside of the United States, so it excludes groups with high percentages of foreign-born individuals who have family abroad
Our study focused on the populations as of July 2020, but for the purposes of this article, we updated our analysis and weighted results to the estimated population as of October 2026
Because estimating the deceased relative population is not a common exercise in our field, we had to make some modeling decisions
We counted only deceased relatives who died after the birth of at least one person still alive; if no one remains who could remember them, we did not include them
Also, we counted deceased persons based on how many relatives they have in the living population

For example, if a deceased 60-year-old man is survived by a spouse, an adult child, a grandchild and a sibling, we count him in the deceased relative population four times, reflecting his being remembered by four living individuals
As such, the deceased relative population we quantified is really a count of how many direct relative ties remain to those who are dead
And finally, we classified deceased relatives according to their age at death
We believe this represents the age many people will most clearly remember their deceased loved ones
Of course, we categorize the living population by their current age
Deceased relatives of today’s Americans Our results included several key findings
First, the deceased relative population is large
Our model estimated that the living Black and white populat,ion representing about 217 million people , had 755 million ties to deceased close relatives
That’s a population more than three times the size of the living population
For every under-15-year-old out trick-or-treating on Halloween, there are about 21 deceased relatives remembered
Second, our model shows that, on average, the deceased relatives died 25 years ago
That the average deceased relative has been remembered for a quarter of a century makes it clear that loved ones are often suspended in memory for years, even decades, after their deaths
Third, over half of the deceased relative population was born more than 100 years ago – even before the term “trick-or-treating” took hold in the U.S
Around 10% of the deceased relatives were born before 1900, with 140,000 of them born before the Civil War – these are the remembered grandparents of today’s oldest individuals
These results speak to how generations of the seemingly long ago past still have a direct tie to the living
The Halloween season reminds us of ghosts, spirits and ancestors

Whatever their beliefs, many Americans also carry relationships with people who are no longer alive: grandparents whose recipes they still make, parents whose advice they still hear, spouses whose absence shapes their days
These relationships are deeply personal, but together they form a vast and previously unstudied shadow population
By quantifying and characterizing the deceased relative population, our research reveals just how many people no longer appear in the census yet remain an integral part of our social world

<title>UN peacekeepers prepare to exit Lebanon after 70 years – leaving behind a worrying security vacuum</title>
    <content type="html"><p>For nearly 70 years, the blue helmets of United Nations’ peacekeepers have dotted the landscape of southern Lebanon. But those days may soon be over.</p>

<p>Under Israeli and American pressure, the U.N. Security Council unanimously voted in August to end the mandate establishing <a href="https://www.securitycouncilreport.org/whatsinblue/2025/08/un-interim-force-in-lebanon-unifil-vote-on-final-mandate-renewal-and-drawdown.php">the United Nations Interim Force in Lebanon, or UNIFIL</a>.</p>

<p>It means the 7,565 members of UNIFIL deployed in Lebanon – <a href="https://unifil.unmissions.org/en/unifil-troop-contributing-countries">representing about 46 countries</a> – will depart the country no later than Dec. 31, 2026.</p>

<p>The end of the U.N. presence comes at a pivotal time. Israel and Lebanon have already held <a href="https://zoryaninstitute.org/scholar-corner/lebanon-israel-are-the-negotiations-dead-or-just-stalled/">seven rounds of negotiations</a> aimed at bringing a lasting peace to a region that has suffered from decades of conflict. </p>

<p>Brokered by the United States, these talks that led to the signing of the <a href="https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesman/2026/06/trilateral-framework-between-the-united-states-of-america-the-state-of-israel-and-the-republic-of-lebanon">Trilateral Framework in June 2026</a> call for the disarmament of Hezbollah, the Israeli withdrawal from all Lebanese lands and the settlement of all disputes over borders. Yet all of these conditions are still some way off from completion – and <a href="https://theconversation.com/hezbollah-degraded-weakened-but-not-yet-disarmed-destabilizes-lebanon-once-again-277327">beset by a series of barriers</a>.</p>

<p>As such, the departure of the United Nations peacekeeping forces raises serious concerns. The potential for a security vacuum looms large in south Lebanon, especially given that <a href="https://qna.org.qa/en/news/news-details?id=israeli-forces-launch-fresh-attacks-in-southern-lebanon&amp;date=6/10/2026">Israel continues to bomb Lebanon</a> despite a <a href="https://www.state.gov/releases/office-of-the-spokesperson/2026/04/ten-day-cessation-of-hostilities-to-enable-peace-negotiations-between-israel-and-lebanon">ceasefire that has nominally been in place since April 16, 2026</a>. </p>

<p>As a <a href="https://theconversation.com/profiles/mireille-rebeiz-1503505">scholar of Middle East Studies</a>, I know that UNIFIL has never been a permanent solution. But I fear that its termination creates more problems than it solves, especially when there are no clear replacements or post-UNIFIL security arrangements in place. </p>

<h2>The UN in Lebanon</h2>

<p>While the U.N. had had an <a href="https://peacekeeping.un.org/sites/default/files/past/unogilbackgr.html">on-the-ground presence in Lebanon to handle civil strife since the 1950s</a>, its role in mediating between Lebanon and Israel started later.</p>

<p>In 1978, after a series of attacks on Israel organized by Palestinian fighters in Lebanon, Israel invaded and occupied the south in what was known as <a href="https://www.idf.il/en/mini-sites/wars-and-operations/operation-litani/">Operation Litani</a>. As a result, the United Nations Security Council <a href="https://unifil.unmissions.org/en/unifil-timeline">established UNIFIL</a> to monitor Israel’s withdrawal from south Lebanon and to restore peace at the Lebanese–Israeli border.</p>

<p>Israel’s occupation of south Lebanon lasted <a href="https://www.theguardian.com/world/2000/may/24/israelandthepalestinians.lebanon">more than two decades</a>. Following its withdrawal on May 25, 2000, the U.N. set the <a href="https://news.un.org/en/story/2026/02/1166875">Blue Line</a> – a 75-mile (120 km) demarcation line created for the practical purpose of confirming Israeli withdrawal from south Lebanon. It was not an official border but a buffer zone monitored by the U.N. peacekeepers.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767812/original/file-20261022-50-q5sf4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A group of soldiers stand next to a airplane with 'Air France' written on it." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767812/original/file-20261022-50-q5sf4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767812/original/file-20261022-50-q5sf4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=391&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767812/original/file-20261022-50-q5sf4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=391&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767812/original/file-20261022-50-q5sf4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=391&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767812/original/file-20261022-50-q5sf4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=491&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767812/original/file-20261022-50-q5sf4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=491&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767812/original/file-20261022-50-q5sf4a.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=491&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>UNFIL and the Blue Line served as geographic and diplomatic focal points in the <a href="https://www.britannica.com/event/2006-Lebanon-War">2006 war</a> between <a href="https://theconversation.com/does-hezbollah-represent-lebanon-and-what-impact-will-the-death-of-longtime-leader-hassan-nasrallah-have-240062">Hezbollah</a> – an Iranian-backed militia operating from Lebanon – and Israel. </p>

<p>Resolution 1701 of the Security Council, which brought an end to the 2006 war, <a href="https://unifil.unmissions.org/en/unifil-timeline">dramatically expanded the UNIFIL role in Lebanon</a>; the number of troops went from 2,000 to 15,000 authorized military personnel.</p>

<p>Its mandate also changed to include monitoring the ceasefire and documenting its violations, coordinating with Lebanon’s military and functioning as the only direct communication channel between the Lebanese and Israeli militaries. UNIFIL also offered humanitarian aid to the affected civilian population of south Lebanon. </p>

<p>Yet UNIFIL’s role never altered the basic lack of peace on the Israeli-Lebanese border. Over 50 years, <a href="https://theconversation.com/israeli-threats-to-occupy-or-annex-south-lebanon-dust-off-a-decades-old-playbook-279704">Israel invaded Lebanon numerous times</a>. And since 2000, <a href="https://theconversation.com/does-hezbollah-represent-lebanon-and-what-impact-will-the-death-of-longtime-leader-hassan-nasrallah-have-240062">Hezbollah has flourished in south Lebanon</a>. </p>

<p><iframe id="PEbmQ" class="tc-infographic-datawrapper" src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/PEbmQ/7/" height="400px" width="100%" style="border: 0;" scrolling="no" frameborder="0" title="A map of Lebanon"></iframe></p>

<h2>A checkered history of interventions</h2>

<p>As UNIFIL prepares to depart, it’s unclear what will fill the looming security vacuum. It could be filled by non-U.N. troops, but Lebanon’s past shows the risks inherent to international peacekeeping missions. </p>

<p>In 1982, after Israel invaded Lebanon and occupied Beirut with the intention of eliminating the Palestinian militant threat, Lebanese authorities called on Western powers for help. In August, the governments of the U.S., France, Italy and the United Kingdom created a <a href="https://www.history.navy.mil/browse-by-topic/wars-conflicts-and-operations/middle-east/lebanon.html">multinational peacekeeping force</a> designed to restore peace and stop the fighting between the Lebanese, Palestinians and Israelis. </p>

<p>But on <a href="https://www.marines.mil/News/Marines-TV/videoid/634642/dvpTag/Beirut/">Oct. 23, 1983</a>, the multinational peacekeeping force was the target of a dual suicide attack that killed 241 American service members and 58 French paratroopers.  </p>

<p>To this day, the attack – claimed by the pro-Iranian <a href="https://www.britannica.com/event/1983-Beirut-barracks-bombings">Islamic Jihad</a> – remains the <a href="https://www.arlingtoncemetery.mil/Explore/Monuments-and-Memorials/Beirut-Barracks">deadliest single-day incident for the U.S. Marine Corps</a> since the Battle of Iwo Jima in 1945. </p>

<p>In addition to Israel, interventions in Lebanon have also come from another neighboring country.</p>

<p>In 1976, the Syrian military intervened during Lebanon’s civil war to put an end to sectarian violence. Nearly three decades of occupation followed, and troops were withdrawn only following the <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/world-middle-east-60691507">assassination of Lebanese Prime Minister Rafik Hariri in 2005</a> and the subsequent <a href="https://nvdatabase.swarthmore.edu/content/lebanese-campaign-democracy-independence-intifada-or-cedar-revolution-2005">Cedar Revolution</a>.</p>

<h2>What next for Lebanon</h2>

<p>With the absence of an internal Lebanese consensus, the arrival of any international peacekeeping force to replace the exiting UNIFIL will be perceived by many Lebanese as a top-down imposition. </p>

<p>Moreover, the situation on the ground makes it dangerous for any international force to successfully operate. Israel is reportedly occupying <a href="https://apnews.com/projects/israel-expansion-maps/">over 10% of Lebanon’s territories</a>, <a href="https://www.bbc.com/news/articles/cge41d19gq9o">including</a> multiple permanent bases and outposts in southern Lebanese territory. </p>

<p>Hezbollah, meanwhile, <a href="https://www.reutersconnect.com/item/lebanon-hezbollah-leader-reaffirms-refusal-to-disarm-vows-continued-resistance-against-israel/dGFnOnJldXRlcnMuY29tLDIwMjY6bmV3c21sX09XU0hCQzExOTAwNDM">refuses to disarm</a>.  </p>

<p>Finally, the fate of Lebanon-Israel <a href="https://zoryaninstitute.org/scholar-corner/lebanon-israel-are-the-negotiations-dead-or-just-stalled/">direct negotiations is unclear</a>. Recently, the countries held military talks in Florida, but <a href="https://www.naharnet.com/stories/323237-little-expected-from-lebanon-israel-military-talks-in-florida/print">little is expected from them</a>.</p>

<p>Yet a number of efforts are ongoing despite the difficult circumstances surrounding UNIFIL’s withdrawal. On June 25, French President Emmanuel Macron and Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni announced an “<a href="https://www.elysee.fr/en/emmanuel-macron/2026/06/25/franco-italian-joint-statement#">international coalition to support Lebanon</a>” to reinforce Lebanon’s sovereignty and help prevent a security vacuum in south Lebanon.  </p>

<p>In parallel, the <a href="https://www.euronews.com/2026/10/12/eu-agrees-new-security-mission-in-lebanon-as-un-peacekeepers-prepare-to-leave">European Union Foreign Ministers</a> approved a new civilian-military mission aimed at advising and training the Lebanese military and police personnel. </p>

<p>But these appear to be limited operations that aren’t designed to replace UNIFIL. </p>

<p>U.S. President Donald Trump, meanwhile, has previously <a href="https://www.washingtoninstitute.org/policy-analysis/us-should-not-encourage-syria-enter-lebanon">proposed that Syria enter Lebanon</a> to help end the violence and execute “a surgical attack on Hezbollah.”</p>

<p>But given the past experience of Syrian occupation, this proposal would certainly not be welcomed by the Lebanese people.</p>

<h2>Remaining questions</h2>

<p>Although Lebanese security is a paramount concern regarding the impending withdrawal of UNIFIL, it’s not the only potential risk.</p>

<p>UNIFIL <a href="https://english.aawsat.com/arab-world/5331838-end-unifil-mission-impacts-hundreds-jobs-south-lebanon">employs many Lebanese civilians and is a steady consumer of local goods and services</a>. It also provides humanitarian aid to the region. </p>

<p>And the departure of UNIFIL may further erode Lebanon sovereignty by opening the door for the sharing of security by neighbors – and former occupiers – Syria and Israel.</p>

<p>This is all the more worrying given that the <a href="https://www.thenationalnews.com/opinion/comment/2026/03/24/theres-only-so-much-lebanons-army-can-do-against-hezbollah-it-needs-to-make-every-move-count/">Lebanese armed forces</a> are poorly trained, have a poor record as a fighting force and will be susceptible to attacks from Hezbollah fighters and sympathizers, which might trigger sectarian violence in the country. </p>

<figure class="align-center ">
            <img alt="A man in a blue helmet holds a large gun" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767716/original/file-20261022-50-9qgits.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767716/original/file-20261022-50-9qgits.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=408&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767716/original/file-20261022-50-9qgits.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=408&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767716/original/file-20261022-50-9qgits.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=408&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767716/original/file-20261022-50-9qgits.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=512&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767716/original/file-20261022-50-9qgits.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=512&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767716/original/file-20261022-50-9qgits.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=512&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px">
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">A UNIFIL peacekeeper  in South Lebanon in 1985.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/unifil-in-south-lebanon-news-photo/948111474?phrase=UNIFIL&amp;adppopup=true">Roland Neveu/Gamma-Rapho via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In the vacuum left by U.N. forces, some Lebanese military personnel might simply decide that opposing Hezbollah is too risky altogether.</p>

<p>All of these factors make what comes next for Lebanon after UNIFIL’s departure as opaque as it is worrying for those concerned about the country’s well-being. </p>

<p>For the sake of Lebanese sovereignty, the twin goals of disarming Hezbollah and ensuring Israel’s withdrawal from Lebanese territory remain paramount. Yet it’s unclear who will take on those duties absent a stronger Lebanese state.</p>

<p>For all of its inability to prevent wars, invasions and violations of ceasefires, UNIFIL’s presence guaranteed a degree of Lebanese sovereignty over its lands and served as a reminder of the international community’s commitment to peace in the region. An effective replacement force would at least have to do the same.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/293159/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>PHP is in the foundation of 70% of websites – here’s what it is and why a flaw in the software is a major hacking threat</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767981/original/file-20261023-50-hmz6ge.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=164%2C657%2C4236%2C2824&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">PHP is a key building block of most websites.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/photo/conceptual-image-of-geometric-blocks-royalty-free-image/1363978452?phrase=plain%20building%20blocks%20one%20red%20block">Richard Drury/DigitalVision via Getty Images</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>Governments and organizations around the world began scrambling on Oct. 21, 2026, <a href="https://www.cnbc.com/2026/10/22/php2shell-vulnerability-what-is-it-and-is-your-data-at-risk.html">to fix a vulnerability</a> in software that runs their websites, a bug that could give hackers access to data and control of websites. The flaw in PHP, the programming language that powers much of today’s web, prompted urgent warnings <a href="https://www.nsa.gov/Press-Room/Press-Releases-Statements/Press-Release-View/Article/4630238/nsa-advisory-critical-patches-recommended-for-php-vulnerabilities/">from the U.S. National Security Agency</a>, cybersecurity agencies and software vendors. </p>

<p>A researcher at <a href="https://calif.io/">Calif</a>, a security research firm, <a href="https://www.wsj.com/tech/cybersecurity/ai-just-found-a-bug-that-puts-up-to-70-of-the-worlds-websites-at-risk-fd0902ea">found the flaw in August 2026</a> using an advanced artificial intelligence model from OpenAI. The firm alerted the nonprofit that manages PHP. However, word of the flaw leaked before the PHP organization released patches for its software, and according to Amazon Web Services officials, <a href="https://arstechnica.com/security/2026/10/hackers-got-a-four-day-head-start-on-epic-php2shell-vulnerability/">hackers began “broadly” attempting to exploit it</a>.</p>

<p>The vulnerability has implications far beyond a single company or platform, because PHP is a key piece of software that helps run millions of websites. So, what is PHP, what role did AI play in uncovering the vulnerability, and should the average user worry?</p>

<h2>PHP: The foundation of the web</h2>

<p><a href="https://www.php.net/">PHP</a> is a programming language that <a href="https://www.britannica.com/technology/PHP">powers most websites</a>. For a modern website to provide dynamic content, visual elements and searchable features, a program must run on the web server and take user input, whether that is entering a web address or clicking links and buttons. Estimates suggest that <a href="https://www.reuters.com/technology/what-is-php-why-did-it-take-government-websites-offline-2026-10-21/">around 70% of websites</a> run on PHP.</p>

<p>PHP operates on a web server <a href="https://www.php.net/manual/en/mongodb.overview.php">in two main parts</a>: the core PHP system – the engine and <a href="https://technav.ieee.org/topic/runtime-library/">runtime libraries</a> – and the individual PHP scripts, which are the custom programs that actually implement a website. When you interact with a website, PHP scripts run, take user input and <a href="https://www.php.net/manual/en/introduction.php">produce the output</a> your web browser displays.  </p>



<h2>The vulnerability</h2>

<p>The current security issue sits directly <a href="https://www.abstract.security/blog/php2shell-critical-php-rce-vulnerabilities-cve-2026-109618-and-cve-2026-109619">in the core PHP system</a> and the libraries it uses. When a vulnerability exists at this deep level, it can allow an adversary to exploit the system. In this case, they can run unauthorized commands on the computer hosting the website, which allows attackers to access data and gain full control of the website.</p>

<p>This vulnerability is not a mistake in an individual website’s code. The issue lies in the core PHP system, making every unpatched system running PHP vulnerable. Since websites are accessible to anyone on the internet, adversaries can easily find PHP-based websites using automated tools. From there, they can run an exploit program that takes advantage of the vulnerability.</p>

<p>This exploit code is called PHP2Shell. This name comes from the fact that the exploit gives the attacker “shell access,” a cybersecurity term for direct command-line control of the computer running the website. Shell access bypasses the website interface, giving adversaries a window to enter commands and access all the website’s data.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/K8EXJIDk-K4?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">How PHP2Shell works.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>AI: A double-edged sword</h2>

<p>What makes this vulnerability particularly interesting is how it was discovered. This exploit came to light through a process known as coordinated disclosure, in which cybersecurity researchers report the flaw to PHP developers before publicizing it.</p>

<p>This discovery shows the power of AI in cybersecurity. For decades, finding subtle software flaws required large teams of specialists manually reviewing code. Today’s AI systems can examine vast codebases and identify unusual patterns in hours or days. These models can analyze millions of lines of code in seconds, spotting subtle memory management bugs that human auditors might miss over decades of software development. The PHP vulnerability has existed in the core PHP code for over a decade, and AI helped researchers find it.</p>

<p>However, this also shows that attackers can use these same tools to locate and exploit vulnerabilities. The same reasoning capabilities that help security researchers find flaws first can also let attackers rapidly scan the web for vulnerable targets and automate the creation of tools to exploit the vulnerabilities. </p>

<p>This illustrates why it is so critical for security teams to use AI to find vulnerabilities and report them safely and actively. AI can also help release <a href="https://www.cisa.gov/news-events/alerts/2026/10/21/critical-vulnerabilities-php-require-immediate-patching">patches that mitigate these vulnerabilities</a>. </p>

<h2>Should you worry?</h2>

<p>Many government agencies, universities, hospitals and businesses <a href="https://www.reuters.com/technology/what-is-php-why-did-it-take-government-websites-offline-2026-10-21/">rely on PHP-based systems</a>. While individual internet users are unlikely to be directly affected, organizations that delay patching could expose sensitive data, risk having their operations disrupted or give attackers a foothold into larger networks.</p>

<p>PHP runs entirely on remote web servers. If you are an everyday internet user visiting websites, you do not need to download a patch or fix your personal computer. </p>

<p>However, if you manage a website, blog or server, even a small site built on popular content management systems such as WordPress, you should check your server administration panel or web host immediately to ensure your PHP software is updated to the latest patched version. If a third party hosts your website, check with them to see whether they have patched for these vulnerabilities.</p>

<p>The PHP2Shell discovery illustrates a new reality for cybersecurity. In our interconnected world, keeping web infrastructure secure is a continuous race. As AI tools become standard for both cyber defenders and online adversaries, maintaining fast patching habits remains our most essential defense.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294999/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

<title>Why ultra-Orthodox parties hold so much sway in Israeli politics</title>
    <content type="html"><figure><img src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767707/original/file-20261022-50-6glxab.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;rect=0%2C1%2C8640%2C5760&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1050&amp;h=700&amp;fit=crop" /><figcaption><span class="caption">Israeli police disperse ultra-Orthodox Jews blocking a road during a protest against the army draft in Jerusalem on Oct. 8, 2026.</span> <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/IsraelDraft/31a12cfd2d2f49429a233d46a8f5dd69/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=israel%20protest%20draft&amp;currentItemNo=8&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg</a></span></figcaption></figure><p>On Oct. 20, 2026, a week before Israel’s elections, dozens of men <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/israel-ultra-orthodox-jewish-men-arrested-evading-military-draft/">were detained on suspicion of evading the draft</a> – arrests that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu <a href="https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-912252">called “unacceptable</a>.”</p>

<p>The young men attend ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, religious schools, whose students were long exempt from the military service mandatory for most Israelis. <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/israel-supreme-court-rules-religious-seminary-students-must-be-drafted-military-2024-06-25/">A 2024 court ruling</a> that Haredi men must be drafted alongside other Jewish youth intensified the conscription debate. Netanyahu’s government has failed to either legalize the draft exemption or enforce the court’s ruling, though he has said Haredim who are not studying <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/netanyahu-arrests-of-haredi-draft-dodgers-a-deliberate-attempt-to-harm-their-recruitment/">should enlist</a>.</p>

<p>With Israel’s military fighting in several conflicts, those exemptions have become increasingly unpopular: The vast majority of Jewish voters <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2016/03/Israel-Survey-Full-Report.pdf">want Haredi communities to share the burden</a>. Haredi political parties, however, are key potential coalition members as Netanyahu attempts to secure his political future. Although a relatively small percentage of the population, the Haredim hold disproportionate sway in Israel’s parliamentary system.</p>

<h2>Growing population</h2>

<p>Haredi Jews <a href="https://theconversation.com/jewish-denominations-a-brief-guide-for-the-perplexed-207297">strictly observe Jewish religious law</a> and often disapprove of liberal interpretations. They typically live in Haredi-majority neighborhoods where large families are the norm – <a href="https://blogs.timesofisrael.com/demographic-reversal-israel-chooses-life/">six children, on average</a> – and about half of the men <a href="https://en.idi.org.il/haredi/2025/?chapter=63079">devote themselves to full-time religious study</a>. The <a href="https://en.idi.org.il/haredi/2025/?chapter=63078">poverty rate is 33%</a>, more than double the percentage for non-Haredi Jews.</p>

<p>The Israeli public is <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/by-2050-almost-one-in-four-israelis-will-be-ultra-orthodox-study-indicates/">about 14% Haredi</a>, but the community is growing quickly because of its high birth rate. Projections by the Central Bureau of Statistics estimate that almost <a href="https://en.idi.org.il/articles/63385">a quarter of Israelis will be Haredi</a> by 2050. </p>

<p>Haredi communities are diverse and represented by two main political parties. Haredim who are Ashkenazi – Jews whose ancestors <a href="https://theconversation.com/fiddler-on-the-roof-may-be-many-americans-image-of-judaism-but-american-jews-heritage-is-stunningly-diverse-229170">came from northern and eastern Europe</a> – are linked to United Torah Judaism, or UTJ. Those who are Sephardi or Mizrachi, meaning their ancestors <a href="https://theconversation.com/on-passover-some-sephardic-jews-revisit-not-only-the-story-of-their-ancestors-but-also-their-ladino-language-278290">came from the Iberian Peninsula</a> and the Middle East, are linked to Shas. </p>

<p>A third Haredi party, Haredi Public, was <a href="https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/article-902998">formed in July 2026</a>. The party says it will represent Haredim <a href="https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-911772">who feel underserved by Shas and UTJ</a>, emphasizing employment and poverty, housing development and the education system. Unlike the other two Haredi parties, it has <a href="https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-911477">included women</a> on its candidate list.</p>

<h2>Conservative allies</h2>

<p>Elections for the Israeli parliament, the Knesset, use <a href="https://israelpolicyforum.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/How-Do-Israeli-Elections-Work.pdf">a proportional representation system</a>. Any party that receives more than 3.25% of votes receives seats based on the fraction of votes it received. Each party allocates its seats to members based on a list of candidates published before elections.</p>

<p>Having multiple parties with similar target demographics risks dividing the vote, leaving that group with fewer representatives in the Knesset. Shas and UTJ have <a href="https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-911320">agreed to share their surplus votes</a> in the 2026 election to maximize their overall seat share.</p>

            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767765/original/file-20261022-50-6rnhml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="A few men walk through a plaza in front of a building with a large poster of a man with a white beard and dark glasses." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767765/original/file-20261022-50-6rnhml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767765/original/file-20261022-50-6rnhml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767765/original/file-20261022-50-6rnhml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767765/original/file-20261022-50-6rnhml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767765/original/file-20261022-50-6rnhml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767765/original/file-20261022-50-6rnhml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767765/original/file-20261022-50-6rnhml.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

<p>Because of the low electoral threshold, many parties are able to win seats. No Israeli party has ever attained the 50% share needed to control parliament by itself. As in other countries with similar systems, it is very common for parties to form coalitions and govern as a team. </p>

<p>Likud, one of the major conservative parties, has led most <a href="https://www.gov.il/apps/pmo/history/historyGovernmentsEn.html">governing coalitions for the past two decades</a>, with party leader Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister. Haredi parties are seen as <a href="https://en.idi.org.il/articles/49206">strong conservative allies</a>, and they have been key coalition members for Likud administrations. Today, as Netanyahu <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/netanyahu-races-unify-israels-right-wing-bid-avert-election-defeat-2026-09-08/">faces challenges from other right-wing parties</a> over his handling of Oct. 7, 2023, and several wars, Likud may need them even more. </p>

<h2>Landmark ruling</h2>

<p>The fact that Likud has needed Haredi parties to form coalitions has given them negotiating power. For many years, one of their priorities has been <a href="https://www.haaretz.com/israel-news/2026-07-14/ty-article-magazine/.premium/from-1948-to-october-7-the-ultra-orthodox-draft-remains-israels-fault-line/0000019f-3bd2-d238-a9ff-bfd63adf0000">draft exemptions for religious education</a>.</p>

<p>Military service is mandatory for most groups in Israel, although <a href="https://www.cfr.org/backgrounders/what-know-about-arab-citizens-israel">Muslim and Christian Arab citizens</a> are generally exempted. Jewish Israelis see conscription as a unifying experience and a <a href="https://en.idi.org.il/articles/64447">costly demonstration</a> of commitment to the state. Starting at age 18, most women serve two years and most men serve almost three years. Former soldiers can be called up as reservists into their 40s, depending on their training.</p>

<p>For decades, Haredi men received de facto exemptions. It was, effectively, one of several government arrangements that subsidize Haredi communities. Religious schools for teen boys and married men receive <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/the-high-courts-yeshiva-funding-ruling-goes-into-effect-today-what-does-it-mean/">government payments</a> for each student. Given the communities’ low employment rates, large families and high poverty rates, many <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/government-data-said-to-show-haredim-far-likelier-than-other-jews-to-get-state-subsidies/">families rely</a> <a href="https://en.idi.org.il/articles/66049">on public support</a>.</p>

<p>In 2024, Israel’s Supreme Court ruled that a blanket exemption from military service for Haredim <a href="https://www.reuters.com/world/middle-east/israel-supreme-court-rules-religious-seminary-students-must-be-drafted-military-2024-06-25/">was not legal</a>. Netanyahu’s government struggled to enact a compromise between those who favored drafting Haredim and the Haredi parties; the failure to find a lasting legal way to exempt Haredi men led Shas and UTJ to <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/shas-quits-its-coalition-posts-to-protest-failure-to-legislate-haredi-draft-exemption/">leave the Likud-led coalition</a> in 2025.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767771/original/file-20261022-50-zph53l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Men in black suits and white shirts hold signs that say, 'We will go to jail, but not to the army.'" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767771/original/file-20261022-50-zph53l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767771/original/file-20261022-50-zph53l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767771/original/file-20261022-50-zph53l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767771/original/file-20261022-50-zph53l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767771/original/file-20261022-50-zph53l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767771/original/file-20261022-50-zph53l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767771/original/file-20261022-50-zph53l.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Ultra-Orthodox Jewish men protest military recruitment by blocking a road in Bnei Brak, near Tel Aviv, Israel, on July 16, 2024.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/detail/IsraelOrthodox/cd5aaf2b4b114fca919999c7a1ae643c/photo?vs=false&amp;displayquery=netanyahu%20draft&amp;currentItemNo=5&amp;startingItemNo=0&amp;sourceLocation=Search">AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<h2>Growing tensions</h2>

<p>Nonetheless, this ruling has not led to mass conscription. </p>

<p>Haredi groups have <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/report-netanyahu-asked-haredi-parties-to-cancel-anti-draft-protests-fearing-optics/">held public protests</a>, and many have ignored draft notices. While tens of thousands of men are <a href="https://www.ynetnews.com/jewish-world/article/rjj00e77hzx">draft eligible but not serving</a>, and most of them are Haredi, fewer than 500 evaders have been arrested in 2026. Netanyahu argues <a href="https://www.cbsnews.com/news/israel-ultra-orthodox-jewish-men-arrested-evading-military-draft/">against arrests</a>, saying they discourage men from enlisting without coercion.</p>

<p>In July 2026, at the urging of Haredi parties, the government <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-passes-law-banning-arrests-of-haredi-draft-dodgers-legitimizing-ongoing-non-enlistment/">passed a law</a> to temporarily prevent arresting draft evaders. Some members of Netanyahu’s governing coalition opposed the law, however, and right-wing opposition parties <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/knesset-passes-law-banning-arrests-of-haredi-draft-dodgers-legitimizing-ongoing-non-enlistment/">filed petitions to challenge it in court</a>.</p>

<p>Former Prime Minister Naftali Bennett – leader of the Together alliance, and seen as a key contender to oust Netanyahu – has threatened to <a href="https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/article-911359">cut subsidies to the Haredi community</a> if they continue to defy the draft. Gadi Eisenkot, leader of the centrist Yashar party, <a href="https://www.jpost.com/israel-election-2026/article-912291">is another top contender to replace Netanyahu</a>. He has proposed allowing <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/liveblog_entry/eisenkot-met-gafni-after-haredi-factions-rabbi-called-to-dissolve-knesset-last-week-report/">3% of Haredi men exemptions to study</a>, while drafting the majority.</p>

<p>As the number of conflict zones increases – Gaza, southern Lebanon and Iran, as well as deployments in the West Bank – the unequal burden of <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/idf-manpower-chief-extension-of-service-period-doesnt-replace-need-for-more-troops/">military participation</a> <a href="https://www.jpost.com/israel-news/politics-and-diplomacy/article-902492">is a growing source of resentment among</a> many conscripted Israelis and their families. <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2016/03/Israel-Survey-Full-Report.pdf">Seven in 10</a> Jewish Israelis favor drafting the Haredim.</p>

<p>Shas and UTJ, however, have declared they will not join a coalition unless it <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/deri-says-like-utj-shas-wont-join-next-government-without-a-draft-exemption-law/">promises to codify the draft exemption into law</a>.</p>

<h2>Shifting coalitions</h2>

<p>When the Haredi parties exited Netanyahu’s coalition, Likud replaced them with <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-032-10253-9">nationalist parties</a> that emphasize the state and Jewish supremacy. Particularly notable was <a href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/world/middle_east/israel-election-netanyahu-ben-gvir/2021/03/19/c3992b7c-85c4-11eb-be4a-24b89f616f2c_story.html">the decision to include the Jewish Power party</a>, an offshoot of an earlier group <a href="https://www.nytimes.com/1988/10/06/world/israel-bans-kahane-party-from-election.html">banned for racism</a>; including Kahanist groups was long seen as <a href="https://blogs.timesofisrael.com/netanyahu-and-the-rise-of-neo-kahanism/">a red line</a>.</p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767776/original/file-20261022-50-7uhd9t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Two men in suits and ties grin and shake hands as several other people watch on." src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767776/original/file-20261022-50-7uhd9t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767776/original/file-20261022-50-7uhd9t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767776/original/file-20261022-50-7uhd9t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767776/original/file-20261022-50-7uhd9t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=400&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767776/original/file-20261022-50-7uhd9t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767776/original/file-20261022-50-7uhd9t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767776/original/file-20261022-50-7uhd9t.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=503&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, seen here with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in 2023, is also head of the Jewish Power party.</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://newsroom.ap.org/home/search?query=netanyahu%20ben-gvir&amp;mediaType=photo">AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Haredi communities, on the other hand, tend to <a href="https://doi.org/10.1007/s41682-022-00139-8">prioritize religious Jewishness</a> over the state. <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/wp-content/uploads/sites/20/2016/03/Israel-Survey-Full-Report.pdf">Most Haredim do not consider</a> <a href="https://theconversation.com/what-is-zionism-the-different-meanings-of-a-contested-term-285771">themselves Zionist</a>, and a small percentage <a href="https://youtube.com/shorts/h9xc8UKH1Ss?si=OAXHLakihZsrI1HZ">are anti-Zionist</a>. They argue that it was <a href="https://www.myjewishlearning.com/article/ultra-orthodox-anti-zionist/">sacrilegious for people to create a state of Israel</a> rather than waiting for God to return Jews to the land of Israel. Where nationalist politicians emphasize the secular state and military service, Haredim see their religious study as service to the Jewish community.</p>

<p>As Likud’s changing coalition shows, Netanyahu’s alliances are strategic rather than ideological. I believe his decision to side with the Haredim on the recent draft legislation suggests his coalition is open to revision after the October 2026 election.</p>

<p>As <a href="https://www.timesofisrael.com/by-2050-almost-one-in-four-israelis-will-be-ultra-orthodox-study-indicates/">the Haredi community grows</a>, its power in the electoral system will become less disproportionate. In a democratic framework, a large social group would deserve proportional representation and influence. As such, the tension between their electoral power, their demands for exemptions and subsidies, and the tolerance of non-Haredi Jews will persist as a political challenge.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/294218/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

    <summary>Ultra-Orthodox Jews, often called Haredim, make up a small but growing percentage of Israel’s population. Still, their political parties wield significant influence.</summary>

body: Israeli police disperse ultra-Orthodox Jews blocking a road during a protest against the army draft in Jerusalem on Oct. 8, 2026

AP Photo/Ohad Zwigenberg On Oct. 20, 2026, a week before Israel’s elections, dozens of men were detained on suspicion of evading the draft – arrests that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu called “unacceptable .” The young men attend ultra-Orthodox, or Haredi, religious schools, whose students were long exempt from the military service mandatory for most Israelis
A 2024 court ruling that Haredi men must be drafted alongside other Jewish youth intensified the conscription debate
Netanyahu’s government has failed to either legalize the draft exemption or enforce the court’s ruling, though he has said Haredim who are not studying should enlist
With Israel’s military fighting in several conflicts, those exemptions have become increasingly unpopular: The vast majority of Jewish voters want Haredi communities to share the burden
Haredi political parties, however, are key potential coalition members as Netanyahu attempts to secure his political future
Although a relatively small percentage of the population, the Haredim hold disproportionate sway in Israel’s parliamentary system
Growing population Haredi Jews strictly observe Jewish religious law and often disapprove of liberal interpretations
They typically live in Haredi-majority neighborhoods where large families are the norm – six children, on average – and about half of the men devote themselves to full-time religious study
The poverty rate is 33% , more than double the percentage for non-Haredi Jews
The Israeli public is about 14% Haredi , but the community is growing quickly because of its high birth rate
Projections by the Central Bureau of Statistics estimate that almost a quarter of Israelis will be Haredi by 2050
People walk the streets of the ultra-Orthodox neighborhood Mea Shearim in Jerusalem, Israel, on April 18, 2024
AP Photo/Leo Correa Haredi communities are diverse and represented by two main political parties
Haredim who are Ashkenazi – Jews whose ancestors came from northern and eastern Europe – are linked to United Torah Judaism, or UTJ
Those who are Sephardi or Mizrachi, meaning their ancestors came from the Iberian Peninsula and the Middle East, are linked to Shas
A third Haredi party, Haredi Public, was formed in July 2026
The party says it will represent Haredim who feel underserved by Shas and UTJ , emphasizing employment and poverty, housing development and the education system
Unlike the other two Haredi parties, it has included women on its candidate list
Conservative allies Elections for the Israeli parliament, the Knesset, use a proportional representation system
Any party that receives more than 3.25% of votes receives seats based on the fraction of votes it received
Each party allocates its seats to members based on a list of candidates published before elections
Having multiple parties with similar target demographics risks dividing the vote, leaving that group with fewer representatives in the Knesset
Shas and UTJ have agreed to share their surplus votes in the 2026 election to maximize their overall seat share
Orthodox Jews walk past an election campaign banner for the Haredi religious political party Shas, bearing a portrait of former Sephardi Chief Rabbi Ovadia Yosef, in Jerusalem on Oct. 15, 2026
John Wessels/ AFP via Getty Images Because of the low electoral threshold, many parties are able to win seats
No Israeli party has ever attained the 50% share needed to control parliament by itself
As in other countries with similar systems, it is very common for parties to form coalitions and govern as a team
Likud, one of the major conservative parties, has led most governing coalitions for the past two decades , with party leader Benjamin Netanyahu as prime minister
Haredi parties are seen as strong conservative allies , and they have been key coalition members for Likud administrations
Today, as Netanyahu faces challenges from other right-wing parties over his handling of Oct. 7, 2023, and several wars, Likud may need them even more
Landmark ruling The fact that Likud has needed Haredi parties to form coalitions has given them negotiating power
For many years, one of their priorities has been draft exemptions for religious education
Military service is mandatory for most groups in Israel, although Muslim and Christian Arab citizens are generally exempted
Jewish Israelis see conscription as a unifying experience and a costly demonstration of commitment to the state
Starting at age 18, most women serve two years and most men serve almost three years
Former soldiers can be called up as reservists into their 40s, depending on their training
For decades, Haredi men received de facto exemptions
It was, effectively, one of several government arrangements that subsidize Haredi communities
Religious schools for teen boys and married men receive government payments for each student

title: Fear-based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear

<title>Fear-based campaign ads can grab attention, but whether they win votes is less clear</title>
    <content type="html"><p>On a Monday night in September 1964, television viewers <a href="https://livingroomcandidate.org/commercials/1964/peace-little-girl-daisy">watched a little girl counting petals</a> on a flower. Her voice gave way to a man counting down, and then a nuclear blast filled the screen.</p>

<p>The ad <a href="https://www.gilderlehrman.org/sites/default/files/2023-09/Epstein_0.pdf">ran as a paid spot only once</a>, in support of President Lyndon B. Johnson’s reelection campaign. It never mentioned his <a href="https://search.worldcat.org/title/44090431">opponent, republican Barry Goldwater</a>. The ad played on a fear voters already held, <a href="https://ropercenter.cornell.edu/blog/public-opinion-about-using-nuclear-weapons">that Goldwater might start a nuclear war</a>. Republicans protested loudly, Democrats pulled the spot, and the <a href="https://www.smithsonianmag.com/history/how-daisy-ad-changed-everything-about-political-advertising-180958741/">uproar got it rebroadcast</a> in full on network news.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/riDypP1KfOU?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">Formally titled ‘Peace, Little Girl,’ this political commercial was produced for President Lyndon B. Johnson’s 1964 campaign against Barry Goldwater.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>I study how emotional appeals persuade, from how viewers’ moods shape their <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/1041794X.2012.712194">reactions to political ads</a> to how <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-2958.2006.00006.x">anxiety drives people to seek out</a>, and sometimes fail to absorb, information about threats.</p>

<p>The LBJ “Daisy” ad shows why political campaigns to this day <a href="https://www.facebook.com/TCDearborn/posts/republican-us-senate-candidate-mike-rogers-new-ad-targeting-abdul-el-sayed-is-ra/1756483326329553/">continue to reach for fear</a>, and it hints at why the payoff is less predictable than you might think.</p>

<h2>Why campaigns use fear</h2>

<p><a href="https://doi.org/10.1176/appi.ajp.2016.16030353">Fear is an alarm</a>. It tells you something threatening is close. You feel scared when you believe you are at risk from something dangerous that can hurt you.</p>

<p>Anxiety knocks people off autopilot, sharpens attention and sends them looking for new information. That heightened attentiveness may be exactly what a struggling campaign wants.</p>

<p>When political scientists <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=X2Sg8SIAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">Travis Ridout</a> and <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=NIrlYoQAAAAJ&amp;hl">Kathleen Searles</a> <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1467-9221.2010.00819.x">tracked Senate ads</a> from 2004, they found that front-runners often leaned on enthusiasm and pride in their messaging, while candidates who were behind leaned on fear and anger.</p>

<h2>Does fear change votes?</h2>

<p>Sometimes, fear works. </p>

<p>During the 1998 Massachusetts governor’s race, political scientist <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=JPK--icAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">Ted Brader</a> ran a study that embedded campaign ads in a news broadcast and <a href="https://press.uchicago.edu/ucp/books/book/chicago/C/bo3640346.html">changed only the music and images, keeping the words identical</a>. Those changes produced completely different reactions. When a negative ad paired grainy black-and-white images of drug use with tense music, viewers paid closer attention to the spoken message and became more open to reconsidering their chosen candidate.</p>

<p>Fear cues – like a nuclear mushroom cloud – can push viewers to weigh fresh information and reconsider their choice. One surprise: Politically informed citizens were more responsive to these emotional cues than less engaged ones. Fear is not simply a tool for swaying the uninformed, undecided voter. It also reaches people who follow politics closely. Emotion provides the motivation, while knowledge provides the ability to think carefully about the issues and positions and seek out more information.</p>

<p>More broadly, a <a href="https://doi.org/10.1037/a0039729">meta-analysis of over 100 studies</a> found that fear appeals reliably shift attitudes and behavior across health and other domains. For instance, public health researcher <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=PPPSsQoAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">Lucy Popova</a> tested fear-based messages designed to discourage smokers from trying snus, a smokeless tobacco product. She found that when participants perceived a serious threat but also felt capable of acting on it, they <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/10410236.2013.824063">held less favorable attitudes</a> toward snus and were less inclined to try it.</p>

<p>Political attack ads – fear messaging being one type – have a shakier record. A <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-2508.2007.00618.x">review of more than 100 studies</a> found no dependable evidence that negative campaigning wins elections, and some evidence that it lowers positive feelings toward the candidate who sponsors it.</p>

<h2>The critical ingredient is empowerment</h2>

<p>Communication scholar <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=kxXEupgAAAAJ&amp;hl=en">Kim Witte’s</a> research found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1080/03637759209376276">fear motivates action when</a> people believe there is a workable response that they can carry out. When the threat feels big and the solution feels out of reach, <a href="https://theconversation.com/humans-are-hardwired-to-dismiss-facts-that-dont-fit-their-worldview-127168">people protect themselves from the message instead</a>. They tune out, deny the threat or decide the messenger is the problem. </p>

<figure class="align-center zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="Graphic warnings on cigarette packages in Canada" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=450&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/767866/original/file-20261023-50-r2wjkr.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=566&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>
            <figcaption>
              <span class="caption">Gruesome warnings on tobacco products can spark fear – but what’s the next step?</span>
              <span class="attribution"><a class="source" href="https://www.gettyimages.com/detail/news-photo/graphic-warnings-are-displayed-on-the-packaging-of-news-photo/2262538399">Creative Touch Imaging Ltd./NurPhoto via Getty Images</a></span>
            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>For example, picture an ad geared toward adolescent vaping that shows teens in hospital beds with ventilators using scary terms like “popcorn lungs.” If the ad also communicates that vaping can destroy lungs irreversibly, the teen audience is likely to experience extreme fear while at the same time feeling like there’s no way to fix the problem.</p>

<p>My colleagues and I have seen this effect in our own experiments. We found that people who felt highly anxious and also confident they could act <a href="https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1468-2958.2006.00006.x">sought out the most information</a>. Those who felt anxious but lacked that confidence did go looking, yet they recalled very little. Anxiety pushed them to search but got in the way of absorbing what they read.</p>

<p>A campaign that frightens voters without offering a clear step to address the issue could end up producing plenty of anxious attention and very little learning.</p>

<p>Empowerment also helps explain who shows up at the polls. Political scientist <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=1ed6QpkAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=sra">Nicholas Valentino</a> and colleagues found that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0022381610000939">anger boosted voter participation</a> more reliably than anxiety, and anxiety mattered mainly for people who already had the skills and resources to take actions like donate to campaigns, attend rallies, sign petitions and so on.</p>

<h2>Fear plays on prejudice and stereotypes</h2>

<p>Fear does its most reliable work when it attaches to a stereotype voters already carry. The 1988 presidential race provides two classic examples.</p>

<p>One controversial ad, produced in support of Republican George H.W. Bush, showed a mugshot of a Black man. The ad named the man, Willie Horton, and a voiceover explained that he’d committed rape and assault while on a weekend furlough from prison as part of a program run under Massachusetts Governor Michael Dukakis, the Democratic candidate. The spot linked fears about crime to race without saying so directly.</p>

<figure>
            <iframe width="440" height="260" src="https://www.youtube.com/embed/TKXx8GnOgA4?wmode=transparent&amp;start=0" frameborder="0" allowfullscreen=""></iframe>
            <figcaption><span class="caption">The ‘Revolving Door’ ad attacked Democratic presidential candidate Michael Dukakis’ record on crime.</span></figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>Bush’s campaign followed up with the “<a href="https://livingroomcandidate.org/commercials/1988/revolving-door">Revolving Door</a>” ad, which built on that anxiety. It featured stark, black-and-white footage of inmates marching through a revolving gate while a narrator warned that Dukakis had let murderers out of prison on weekend passes. </p>

<p>Political scientist <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=-OEfcQ8AAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">Tali Mendelberg’s</a> research described in “<a href="https://press.princeton.edu/books/paperback/9780691070711/the-race-card">The Race Card</a>” shows that these implicit <a href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/politics/articles/wing-playbook-against-abdul-el-212947742.html">appeals to prejudices and fears are powerful</a>. But they lose much of their force once someone publicly names them as racial. Implicit appeals work because they slip past most voters’ commitment to racial equality; once the racial message is pointed out, voters recognize it and many reject it rather than see themselves as endorsing prejudice.</p>

<p>Gender works in a similar way. </p>

<p>In a national experiment, Public Policy researcher <a href="https://scholar.google.com/citations?user=IzWWT4EAAAAJ&amp;hl=en&amp;oi=ao">Mirya Holman</a> and colleagues found that when campaign <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1065912915624018">messages triggered fears of terrorism</a>, voters turned to their stereotypes of strong leaders as masculine. Those stereotypes hurt a female Democratic candidate, while Republican candidates of either gender were unaffected, since Republicans are already seen as <a href="https://doi.org/10.1177/1065912915624018">tough on security</a>.</p>

<p>A message communicating a threat does not need to name a candidate’s identity to disadvantage them. It simply makes voters reach for the stereotypes they already hold. There’s less systematic research on candidates’ religion, though the same mechanism – fear pushing voters to rely on the stereotypes they already hold about who can keep them safe – predicts similar vulnerability <a href="https://theintercept.com/2026/07/27/abdul-el-sayed-haley-stevens-aipac-senate-michigan/">for Muslim candidates</a>.</p>

<h2>Is fear a more common tactic now?</h2>

<p><a href="https://emotionresearcher.com/the-use-and-consequences-of-emotions-in-politics/">Using fear as a campaign tool</a> is nothing new. </p>

<figure class="align-right zoomable">
            <a aria-label="Zoomable image" href="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=1000&amp;fit=clip"><img alt="black-and-white document 'Some account of the bloody deeds of General Andrew Jackson' with coffin illustrations" src="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=237&amp;fit=clip" srcset="https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=942&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 600w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=942&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1200w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=600&amp;h=942&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 1800w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=45&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1184&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=1 754w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=30&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1184&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=2 1508w, https://images.theconversation.com/files/766847/original/file-20261017-60-mmlx87.jpg?ixlib=rb-4.1.1&amp;q=15&amp;auto=format&amp;w=754&amp;h=1184&amp;fit=crop&amp;dpr=3 2262w" sizes="(min-width: 1466px) 754px, (max-width: 599px) 100vw, (min-width: 600px) 600px, 237px"></a>

            </figcaption>
          </figure>

<p>In 1828, opponents accused presidential candidate <a href="https://reagan.blogs.archives.gov/2022/10/31/american-elections-and-campaigns-1828-a-sign-of-things-to-come/">Andrew Jackson of murder and cannibalism</a>. Both parties have leaned on fear in the television era, from Reagan’s 1984 “<a href="https://livingroomcandidate.org/commercials/1984/bear">Bear</a>” ad about an unnamed Soviet threat, to Democrats’ 1996 warnings that <a href="https://livingroomcandidate.org/websites/cg96/ad1024.htm">seniors’ Medicare was at risk</a>.</p>

<p>What has grown is negativity overall. Political scientist John Geer’s analysis of presidential ads from 1960 to 2004 <a href="https://www.press.uchicago.edu/Misc/Chicago/284996.html">documents that rise</a>, though he also found attack ads, more likely than positive ones, to focus on real issues rather than personal traits. The evidence that fear specifically has increased, as opposed to negativity in general, is less clear.</p>

<p>The current media landscape shifts this dynamic significantly; while traditional <a href="https://www.pewresearch.org/journalism/fact-sheet/network-news/">nightly news broadcasts have seen a decline</a> in viewership, targeted social media feeds have become the emotional battleground.</p>

<p>Recent digital campaign data shows that <a href="https://doi.org/10.1017/S0003055420000696">negative ads are highly prized online</a> because they successfully grab attention by provoking strong emotions like fear and anger. Because platform recommendation systems are heavily <a href="https://theconversation.com/why-social-media-algorithms-send-you-posts-you-dont-like-288792">driven by user activity</a>, campaigns are incentivized to use emotionally charged appeals to maximize viral engagement across feeds.</p>

<p>Fear works less like a switch and more like a spotlight. It grabs attention and opens minds to change, but whether that turns into a vote, a boycott of the ballot box or resentment toward the messenger depends on what comes next.</p><img src="https://counter.theconversation.com/content/292574/count.gif" alt="The Conversation" width="1" height="1" />

excerpt: On a Monday night in September 1964, television viewers watched a little girl counting petals on a flower
body: On a Monday night in September 1964, television viewers watched a little girl counting petals on a flower
Her voice gave way to a man counting down, and then a nuclear blast filled the screen
The ad ran as a paid spot only once , in support of President Lyndon B
It never mentioned his opponent, republican Barry Goldwater
The ad played on a fear voters already held, that Goldwater might start a nuclear war
Republicans protested loudly, Democrats pulled the spot, and the uproar got it rebroadcast in full on network news
Formally titled ‘Peace, Little Girl,’ this political commercial was produced for President Lyndon B
Johnson’s 1964 campaign against Barry Goldwater

I study how emotional appeals persuade, from how viewers’ moods shape their reactions to political ads to how anxiety drives people to seek out , and sometimes fail to absorb, information about threats
The LBJ “Daisy” ad shows why political campaigns to this day continue to reach for fear , and it hints at why the payoff is less predictable than you might think
It tells you something threatening is close
You feel scared when you believe you are at risk from something dangerous that can hurt you
Anxiety knocks people off autopilot, sharpens attention and sends them looking for new information
That heightened attentiveness may be exactly what a struggling campaign wants

When political scientists Travis Ridout and Kathleen Searles tracked Senate ads from 2004, they found that front-runners often leaned on enthusiasm and pride in their messaging, while candidates who were behind leaned on fear and anger
Does fear change votes? Sometimes, fear works

During the 1998 Massachusetts governor’s race, political scientist Ted Brader ran a study that embedded campaign ads in a news broadcast and changed only the music and images, keeping the words identical
Those changes produced completely different reactions
When a negative ad paired grainy black-and-white images of drug use with tense music, viewers paid closer attention to the spoken message and became more open to reconsidering their chosen candidate
Fear cues – like a nuclear mushroom cloud – can push viewers to weigh fresh information and reconsider their choice
One surprise: Politically informed citizens were more responsive to these emotional cues than less engaged ones
Fear is not simply a tool for swaying the uninformed, undecided voter
It also reaches people who follow politics closely
Emotion provides the motivation, while knowledge provides the ability to think carefully about the issues and positions and seek out more information
More broadly, a meta-analysis of over 100 studies found that fear appeals reliably shift attitudes and behavior across health and other domains
For instance, public health researcher Lucy Popova tested fear-based messages designed to discourage smokers from trying snus, a smokeless tobacco product
She found that when participants perceived a serious threat but also felt capable of acting on it, they held less favorable attitudes toward snus and were less inclined to try it
Political attack ads – fear messaging being one type – have a shakier record
A review of more than 100 studies found no dependable evidence that negative campaigning wins elections, and some evidence that it lowers positive feelings toward the candidate who sponsors it
The critical ingredient is empowerment Communication scholar Kim Witte’s research found that fear motivates action when people believe there is a workable response that they can carry out
When the threat feels big and the solution feels out of reach, people protect themselves from the message instead
They tune out, deny the threat or decide the messenger is the problem

Gruesome warnings on tobacco products can spark fear – but what’s the next step? Creative Touch Imaging Ltd./NurPhoto via Getty Images For example, picture an ad geared toward adolescent vaping that shows teens in hospital beds with ventilators using scary terms like “popcorn lungs.” If the ad also communicates that vaping can destroy lungs irreversibly, the teen audience is likely to experience extreme fear while at the same time feeling like there’s no way to fix the problem
My colleagues and I have seen this effect in our own experiments
We found that people who felt highly anxious and also confident they could act sought out the most information
Those who felt anxious but lacked that confidence did go looking, yet they recalled very little
Anxiety pushed them to search but got in the way of absorbing what they read
A campaign that frightens voters without offering a clear step to address the issue could end up producing plenty of anxious attention and very little learning
Empowerment also helps explain who shows up at the polls

Political scientist Nicholas Valentino and colleagues found that anger boosted voter participation more reliably than anxiety, and anxiety mattered mainly for people who already had the skills and resources to take actions like donate to campaigns, attend rallies, sign petitions and so on
