title: Can Trump block the Alaska Senate election?
excerpt: Dan Sullivan (R-AK) at a campaign rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on October 13, 2026. | Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff
body: Dan Sullivan (R-AK) at a campaign rally in Wasilla, Alaska, on October 13, 2026. | Kent Nishimura / AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in  The Logoff , a daily newsletter that helps you stay informed about the Trump administration without letting political news take over your life.  Subscribe here

Welcome to The Logoff: The Trump administration is getting a head start on litigating the midterms.  What’s happening? The administration is asking a federal district court in Alaska to potentially block the certification of Alaska’s US Senate race, should incumbent Sen

Dan Sullivan, a Republican, lose to his Democratic challenger, Mary Peltola.  It’s the first major lawsuit of the 2026 midterms aimed at directly challenging the results, and very likely a sign of things to come after polls close on November 3
What is the administration arguing? Sullivan is currently in a close race against Peltola, a former US representative who polls suggest may hold a slight lead
But the race is complicated by the presence of a second Dan Sullivan, Daniel J
According to the lawsuit, which names Alaska’s state elections director and several state elections entities as defendants, the election could be “tainted by the inclusion on the ballot of Daniel J

Sullivan.”  The suit asks that “Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion,” which it defines as a loss by the incumbent Sullivan in the event that the other Sullivan attracts enough votes to alter the outcome of the election.  What’s the context? The second Dan Sullivan’s appearance on the ballot has already been litigated

After he was initially disqualified from the ballot, the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that he should be included, and he finished third in the state’s August primary (the top four vote-getters appear on Alaska’s general election ballot)
How worried about this should I be? For now, not very

Trump filing lawsuits disputing election results was all but inevitable, even if it’s surprising to see him start this early.  None of that means he’ll succeed: Trump and his allies filed dozens of election lawsuits in 2020 and were largely laughed out of court. (Plus, this particular lawsuit has been assigned to a judge appointed by President Barack Obama.) And with that, it’s time to log off… Hi readers, happy Friday! Here’s some good news to add to a recent string of encouraging headlines about cancer treatment: A new vaccine may reduce the risk of melanoma, the deadliest form of skin cancer, by more than 40 percent, according to the Washington Post
You can read all about it here with a gift link
Thanks for reading, have a great weekend, and we’ll see you on Monday!

title: How worried should I be about the AI hacking panic and “Black October”?
excerpt: An illustration shows a padlock in front of binary code on a laptop screen. | Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained ,
body: An illustration shows a padlock in front of binary code on a laptop screen. | Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP via Getty Images This story appeared in Today, Explained , a daily newsletter that helps you understand the most compelling news and stories of the day

Are we living through “Black October”? Maybe, according to cybersecurity experts who are raising the alarm about AI’s increasingly sophisticated and far-reaching hacking abilities.  This week alone has seen a string of alarming incidents where AI uncovered previously unknown security flaws deep in the infrastructure of the internet

The most concerning involves something called PHP —  a programming language that, according to The Atlantic , is used by “as much as 70 percent of websites.” Cybersecurity researchers used AI to locate a major security breach in the technology
It’s the kind of thing that, when it’s working, is practically invisible

When it stops, though, you really notice it: Government websites in the UK and Europe briefly went down earlier this week after the PHP vulnerability was discovered, as did some sites in the Wikipedia family, the Internet Archive, and many others
The outages weren’t actually the result of a hack, but rather preventative action as web engineers took sites down to fix the vulnerability before it was exploited

But not every PHP-like issue will necessarily be uncovered before it can be exploited by someone using AI tools less ethically, and older websites relying on PHP might go unpatched.  The problem doesn’t stop there, either: Concern is also rising around AI cybersecurity risks to ubiquitous conveniences like online banking

As Axios reported on Thursday , banks are detecting more and more “unauthorized third-party AI agents ” operating inside of their systems.  Those agents are mostly unauthorized by the banks , Axios explains — the holders of the bank account might have given them permission — but it still creates a security risk that executives described as “horrifying,” in part because banks can’t necessarily tell if an agent doesn’t have permission.  It’s a lot to take in, all of it moving extremely quickly, and it’s hard to tell what any of us can do about it as AI labs continue to forge ahead with ever more competent AI models and agents
Luckily, my colleague Adam Clark Estes has some simple recommendations to shore up your own cybersecurity
How do I respond right now? One problem with hackers — even those that happen to be AI agents — is that they can be unpredictable
You won’t know to, say, lock down your Quest Diagnostics records before a breach happens
But whenever you find yourself wondering if your data is safe, that’s a good time to double check that you’ve at least covered your bases
The National Cybersecurity Alliance, a nonprofit dedicated to the safe use of technology, maintains a list of basic online safety practices that everyone should follow
In no particular order, here’s what to pay attention to now: Keep your guard up
AI makes it difficult to know the difference between humans and robots
So be extra careful to avoid engaging in potential phishing scams
Don’t reply to unknown texts, and do due diligence on texts or emails that look like they’re from people you know but just seem off
Don’t give out personal info over the phone, even if it sounds like it’s someone you know
They might be scammers using AI to clone a loved one’s voice
Yes, it’s annoying to pause your phone or computer use for a few minutes to update your software, but this is one of the best ways to get rid of vulnerabilities
Companies like Apple and Google employ huge teams of security experts to spot these in their software and fix them with software updates
Use a password manager or, even better, passkeys
Each of your online accounts should have a unique password that’s at least 16 characters
Yes, it’s impossible to remember that many passwords, so you should also use a password manager like 1Password or the app built into your iPhone or Android device
Just in case you don’t already do it, make sure you use multifactor or two-step authentication for all your accounts, including email and social media
It can be annoying to type in a code or check your email while logging in, but hackers, including AI agents, will have a much harder time getting into your accounts if you take this step
Taking all these measures is not a one-time affair
You have to be vigilant in keeping yourself safe online
Security experts have a term for this that’s almost too specific: cyber hygiene
Like brushing your teeth or taking a shower, take good care of your online life, and do it often
One link for later ➨ Is it still possible to ban gerrymandering? The current US Supreme Court is very, very hostile to getting politics out of congressional map-making
But if Democrats win back power, that doesn’t mean they shouldn’t try
My colleague Ian Millhiser gamed out how they could do it in a way that survives the Court — as well as some approaches that almost certainly wouldn’t fly
But, he writes, the real trick will be finding a solution that functions the way Congress wants it to and can’t be exploited by mapmakers

Before you go… Did you know… that the disease multiple sclerosis is misdiagnosed with surprising frequency ? As many as 15 percent of diagnoses could be false positives — including that of Christina Applegate, who found out this week that she does not have MS despite a 2021 diagnosis
Today’s trivia: Which noble gas is radioactive and has the chemical symbol Rn? (You can find this and other brain puzzles in Vox’s daily crossword
Look for the answer in Monday’s edition.) Yesterday’s trivia: We asked what the plural was for multiple Toyota hybrids
That would be Prii, which Toyota officially confirmed in 2011 after holding a vote.

title: Should you let a chatbot manage your money?
excerpt: A complaint I hear a lot from my millennial peers is that our parents didn’t teach us enough about money
body: A complaint I hear a lot from my millennial peers is that our parents didn’t teach us enough about money
I can say that personal finance wasn’t dinner table conversation in my house, and even as I went off to college and started fending for myself, it was almost a taboo subject

When it came to money, people either had it or they didn’t, and you definitely didn’t talk about it.  Maybe this is why the average American isn’t exactly fluent in personal finance, and the situation is getting worse
Americans can only answer about 50 percent of basic questions about borrowing, savings, and risk on a financial literacy survey, according to a 2026 study by TIAA , a retirement services company
About a third of those surveyed said they have a hard time making ends meet and are debt-constrained
These figures have remained relatively unchanged for nearly a decade , but dropped to their lowest level in this year’s study
It makes sense: It’s hard to learn about money when it’s not taught in schools, and it’s such an intensely private topic

It’s also hard to make good financial decisions when you’re one of the growing number of American households struggling to pay bills , repay debts, and save for the future — and feeling very stressed about it
In a perfect world, each of us could sit down with a financial adviser to get help — but most of us can’t afford that

Instead, average Americans tend to find personal finance tips on TikTok, in Reddit threads, by watching Suze Orman on YouTube or How to Get Rich on Netflix, or by Googling their questions.  Now we have AI tools, too.  With access to an internet’s worth of information and financial advice, ChatGPT, Claude, and other AI chatbots can answer any question you ask

They can help you put together a basic budget or, armed with your bank statements and the details of your student loans and your retirement accounts, tailor solutions to your specific situation. Or, at least, that’s the promise
Key takeaways More people are turning to AI for financial advice : One in five Americans have used AI to help manage their money, and some experts think chatbots could be better than the status quo

AI works best if you know what questions to ask : Those with basic financial literacy will be able to make the most of these tools, while those without it — who might need help the most — could be led astray
Better advice comes with greater risks : Sharing your financial information with a chatbot helps personalize its recommendations
This raises privacy concerns, so you might want to delete your data when you’re done
Think of AI as a financially savvy friend : Chatbots can answer money questions you might be embarrassed to ask someone else and use that context to help build your budget
AI could create a more utopian, more equitable future, where reliable, hyper-personalized advice is just a prompt or two away for people who can’t afford to meet with an expert in real life
But machines are built by people, and there’s good reason to be concerned that these machines will simply replicate the biases and disparities built into our current system

Here’s what experts say about how to make the most of these tools — and how to think about all of the inherent risks of uploading a lot of personal financial information to a chatbot or, worse, giving an AI agent the keys to your bank account

The steep rise, risks, and rewards of AI financial advisers Nearly 20 percent of Americans have used AI tools like ChatGPT for financial advice, and close to 25 percent for Gen Z adults and millennials have tried it, according to an August Gallup poll

These numbers could tick up too: In October, OpenAI started rolling out a dedicated personal finance tool to its ChatGPT Free and Go users in the United States, which effectively means anyone can try it

ChatGPT Finances lets you securely connect your bank account to the tool using a platform called Plaid , and then you can basically have a conversation with the chatbot about your real-time finances down to the penny
It’s like an AI-powered Mint ( RIP ) that you can talk to directly
Regardless of where you encounter a chatbot or how much data you give it, experts say these tools could genuinely help improve financial literacy
You can talk to them about money problems you’re too embarrassed to discuss with friends and family, or ask questions and receive actionable, personalized information
There are real upsides to using AI this way
Taha Choukhmane , an associate professor of finance at the MIT Sloan School of Management, has been studying outcomes when people turn to chatbots for financial advice

In general, these AI tools give pretty good advice, and that advice gets better as people become more practiced in asking the right question , according to research he published earlier this year.  “We were actually quite surprised that relative to the status quo, the average American would be better off if they were to follow the advice,” Choukhmane told me

But he added a caveat: “Just following the advice without understanding the advice puts you at risk of not fully understanding the risk.” But you shouldn’t trust everything a chatbot tells you and should verify everything before making any decisions.  Chatbot advice has some significant limitations
The finance industry has a vested interest in steering you toward certain ways of managing your money, and that typically means selling you products, like loans
If you’ve ever searched for personal finance tips on Google, you’ve probably noticed that a lot of the top results come from banks and other financial institutions
This is by design, according to John Campbell , an economics professor at Harvard

But because AI is aggregating all of that advice, the specific influences and possible bias is less obvious.  “AI is very promising for providing low-cost financial advice in plain English that will arguably be better than what many people would be able to do on their own,” said Campbell, who’s also the co-author of Fixed: Why Personal Finance Is Broken and How to Make It Work for Everyone . “One caveat is that chatbot advice is quite likely — unless a model has been carefully trained — to reflect the average of whatever’s being posted on the internet, and that may or may not be first-rate advice.” An example Campbell gives is the question of when to start taking Social Security benefits

While you’re eligible at age 62, many economists agree that you should delay your benefits, which, based on the way the government calculates your monthly payouts , will allow you to enjoy much higher benefits later in life
But paid financial advisers can recommend starting as early as possible, since waiting longer reduces the amount of money that needs to be managed, which reduces the adviser’s fees
That means there’s a lot of conflicting advice online , much of it supplied by the finance industry

And that’s the information used to train AI models. “The advice is much more mixed,” Campbell said. “And so if a chatbot is learning from that, it may not actually give the best advice.” It can be hard to recognize bad advice anywhere in life, but especially when you’re talking to a machine that’s programmed to please you

A chatbot could encourage you to consider a balance transfer, to lean in on credit card rewards, or to refinance your mortgage — all decisions with upsides and downsides for you, but definite upsides for banks — without you realizing how much of its training data comes from the finance industry selling these products
What’s worse is that if you do end up taking bad advice, it might be years before you realize it
You won’t know that you refinanced a mortgage at a bad time until a better time comes along

title: Designing an AI serving harness built to last
excerpt: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it
body: The next competitive advantage in enterprise AI has less to do with which model you choose than with what you build around it
For the past several years, much of the AI conversation has centered on model capability: bigger models, better reasoning, larger context windows, higher benchmark scores

But as AI moves from experimentation to production, the question facing enterprise leaders has changed—it’s no longer, “what can the model do?”—it’s now, “Can we deliver that intelligence reliably, economically, and at scale?” Increasingly, the answer depends on the serving harness—the engineering system surrounding the model, including the architecture, memory management , scheduling, and optimization decisions that determine how efficiently model intelligence becomes a production capability
For technical executives, that changes where AI investment should go—and what they should demand from the architecture supporting it
Start with the workload, not the model There is no universally “best” model or AI architecture
There is only the right solution for the business problem
A customer-facing assistant optimized for fast responses has fundamentally different requirements from a document-processing pipeline that can run overnight
An internal knowledge application and a high-volume customer service platform may use the same foundation model but require very different serving architectures
The constraints should determine the architecture
That sounds simple, but it runs counter to the way many organizations have approached early AI deployments
During a proof of concept, model accuracy naturally dominates the discussion

Production introduces constraints that are much easier to ignore when only a handful of users are involved: latency, concurrency, memory pressure, GPU utilization, infrastructure cost, and unpredictable traffic
A model that produces marginally better answers is not necessarily the better production choice if it doubles inference costs or cannot meet the application’s latency requirements
Sometimes the smarter engineering decision is the model that delivers exactly the performance the business needs without paying for capability it doesn’t
The objective should be to deploy the right intelligence at the right cost for the workload
That makes serving architecture more than an engineering concern
It becomes an investment decision: where to spend on compute, where to optimize, and where additional model capability simply isn’t worth the cost
Engineer the system, not the model Once AI reaches production, seemingly isolated engineering decisions begin affecting one another
Serving architecture influences memory utilization
Concurrency shapes batching and scheduling, and scheduling affects GPU utilization and latency
Only then can techniques such as quantization, speculative decoding, or optimized attention mechanisms deliver their full value
This interdependence matters because organizations can spend considerably more on infrastructure without solving the constraint limiting performance
During inference, the model’s weights remain fixed, but the key-value (KV) cache grows with active requests and context length
As concurrency increases, a system can run short of usable GPU memory even when compute capacity is still available
Adding more compute without understanding that bottleneck may simply make an inefficient system more expensive
The lesson for technology leaders is broader than memory management: Measure before you optimize
Then determine if another bottleneck emerged
Don’t think of optimization techniques as Pokémon cards: The goal isn’t to collect them all
The goal is to apply the technique that removes the highest-impact constraint while preserving the application’s business requirements
For technology leaders, that demands a different governance question
Instead of asking which AI capabilities the organization can deploy, ask which constraints stand between a proven capability and sustainable business value
Build for change, not today’s benchmark Perhaps the most important reason to invest in the serving harness is that today’s leading model will probably not be tomorrow’s
The architecture surrounding them should make those changes easier to absorb, not force the enterprise to rebuild its AI platform every time technology advances
That makes adaptability an increasingly important outcome of AI strategy

Organizations that build serving systems around workload requirements, clear service-level objectives, and measurable production economics gain the ability to evaluate new models and infrastructure against what the business actually needs
A model change can become an evaluation and configuration decision rather than an architectural reset
EXL researchers have explored these production challenges in greater depth in the EXL Engineering the Harness series
It examines how serving architecture, memory management, scheduling, and inference optimization work together to make enterprise AI more efficient, scalable, and economically sustainable
Increasingly, enterprises have access to many of the same models
Sustainable differentiation comes from how effectively an organization turns that intelligence into business outcomes

title: Making the case for context-aware AI
excerpt: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster
body: Enterprise AI can generate recommendations, automate tasks, and help organizations make decisions faster
But without an understanding of how a business actually operates, even powerful models can miss the constraints and relationships that determine whether a decision is the right one
As companies look to move AI from experimentation into everyday operations, the challenge ahead is giving technology the context to act usefully within complex business processes

For Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis, that context is central to what he calls “decision intelligence.” AI agents can support individual tasks within larger decision-making processes, he argues, but they need to understand the role each task plays and the business conditions surrounding it. “You can’t just do that in a vacuum,” he says
Without the right operational context, agents risk overlooking important constraints, making costly mistakes, or consuming excessive computing resources as they try to work out what they need to know
The solution begins with connecting AI to the processes and data enterprises already use
A contextual layer can help agents understand workflows, operate within defined guardrails, and produce recommendations that people can review and approve
Shah advises organizations to start with a specific business decision, identify its most difficult steps, and test whether AI can improve them
Measuring gains in speed and value can then help determine whether an application is worth scaling
This approach could also change how employees spend their time
Automating repetitive, manual work and coordinating tasks across teams could free people to focus on more complex strategic decisions
Realizing that benefit, however, will require investment in workforce education, so employees can understand AI outputs and their implications instead of just handing decisions over to agents
Looking to the future, Shah sees opportunities extending from routine operational tasks to enterprise-wide planning in areas such as finance, workforce management, marketing, and sales
With the right context, AI could help organizations evaluate options and make consequential decisions more quickly

As Shah puts it, “Now, maybe [resource planning] should not take that much time, and people are actually making the right choices quickly.” This episode of Business Lab is produced in partnership with Celonis

Full Transcript Megan Tatum: From MIT Technology Review, I’m Megan Tatum, and this is Business Lab, the show that helps business leaders make sense of new technologies coming out of the lab and into the marketplace
This podcast is produced in partnership with Celonis
Now, enterprise AI is at something of a crossroads
After years of experimentation, demos, and pilots, leadership teams want clear proof that scaling up will positively impact their bottom line, but many are missing an integral part of the puzzle
By acting without operational context, enterprise AI and AI agents are performing at a significant deficit
They’re applying generalized principles to specialized scenarios and coming up short, leaving business leaders understandably unconvinced and AI’s potential unrealized
My guest today is Devavrat Shah, chief scientist of enterprise AI at Celonis
Megan: Thank you so much for being here with us today

Devavrat, just to start, why is it so crucial that organizations are thinking about operational context as it relates to enterprise AI right now? What makes it such a critical part of that transition I was talking about from experimentation to scale? Devavrat: It’s a fantastic question
And as you correctly noted, we’re at the cusp of becoming experimental to mainstream as far as AI is concerned
As you know, I’ve been teaching AI at MIT as a professor for more than the last two decades, so it’s no surprise that I’m very bullish about AI’s future in enterprises

The way I think about where AI can make the biggest difference in enterprises is in decision making, helping enterprise make decisions, or putting it other way, how do we bring decision intelligence to enterprises? As we think about decisions, how do we make decisions today? Take MIT Tech Review, take Celonis, take MIT, take any large organization
We have different types of decisions we want to make in very broad strokes
There are decisions which are strategic decisions like episodic, other decisions which are operational that need to be done with a high frequency
In either of them, we have some processes in place
You do this first, you do that first, you do that first, you do that first
Many of us play roles within it, what Jensen Huang calls task
And once you get those things done step by step, then you reach decision

Now, it’s those tasks, or what I would call roles, that’s where AI can bring in an atomic manner agentic power so that we can at least parts of decisions, if not all of the decisions, we can augment support and maybe sometimes when it’s a painful automate
And to get to that, to know which role to do, which task to do, we really need to know the context
And that’s why context with AI put together in the right way would bring what I would call decision intelligence to enterprise
And that’s where I think there’ll be the biggest transformation that would come
To drill down into that into a bit more detail, we know many organizations are, as you say, embracing identic AI right now with this potential for increasingly autonomous decision making
If context isn’t introduced in parallel, what are the commercial risks at play? Devavrat: Fantastic
Let’s just take the setting I was describing
